8. **The index is a deliberate deferral, not a gap.** Nothing in §6 reads it; a finding is indexed as an
   ordinary row and every §6 field is kind-specific, exactly like §5's. ADR-0004 intact.
9. **Environment fact — `make aot` fails inside the command sandbox** at the post-link

❓ @product-owner — **how does one card refer to another?** Today it does not, really: a finding
names its section by a free-text `section` label that two independently-writable fields happen to
share, matched by ordinal equality inside a directory `CardLayout.DirectoryFor` gives `Section` and
`Change` scope alike. `--section` is unvalidated and there is **no section-creation verb**, so the
label can name a section card that does not exist. §6 fail-closed on this twice
(`ambiguous-section-label`, and `Unreadable` for a finding raised before its section card exists).

The options, as I read them:

- **A — identity is the reference, and identity resolves.** Reference fields hold card ids
  (`S-0003`, `F-0031`, `R-0007`). A resolver walks `callboard/` — live *and* `changes/archive/` —
  to answer id → card, refusing on a duplicate id. Every §7 reference field, and §6's
  finding→section link, goes through it. Requires a `section create` verb so a section card exists
  to be referenced and `--section` can be validated against it. This is what card-model already
  requires ("a card's identity SHALL remain valid and resolvable after the change that raised it is
  archived") and what 7.7 requires ("every absorbed rule SHALL remain retrievable **by identity**").
  Cost: a resolver block up front, and it pulls 11.1's retrieval-by-identity forward into §7.
- **B — keep free-text labels, make them unique.** Refuse a second `section` card carrying a label
  already used in the same change, so ordinal matching becomes sound and `ambiguous-section-label`
  becomes unreachable. Much cheaper. But a label is change-local, so it cannot express
  `earned_from` pointing at findings in another change or an archived one — which is exactly what a
  repository-scoped rule authored from findings needs — and it does not survive a section rename.
- **C — store repo-relative file paths.** Rejected on spec grounds, recorded so it is not
  re-proposed: archive moves a card's file, and card-model requires identity to survive archive.

I recommend **A**, carved as §7's block A before any register kind ships, and I would fold in the
`workingDirectory` seam (`## NEXT` item 2) while the path-resolution code is open. The open question
inside A is whether `section create` belongs here at all — §5 owned sections and is closed — or
whether that is scope §7 should not take.

**[architect]** Settling the reviewer's architectural note on refusal-code granularity, before block
B mints any more codes. **The worker's two codes stand — but not for the reason it gave.**

The worker's stated rule was "two independently-triggerable facts get two codes". The reviewer is
right that this does not describe this codebase: `--title` and `--role` are two independently
triggerable facts in one handler and share the generic `missing-argument`, separated by message text
alone. Left as stated, that rule would licence a bespoke code for every absent flag in §7's remaining
six blocks, and the supervisor would rightly read the result as codes applied unevenly.

**The rule, stated so it can be applied rather than re-argued:**

> A refusal the **spec names** gets its own code. An **incidental** missing flag gets
> `missing-argument` / `missing-flag-value`.

`hazard-missing-condition` and `hazard-missing-cadence` both clear that bar — register's "Hazards
carry a verification condition" mandates both fields and gives the condition its own scenario
("refuses **and states the condition it requires**"), so a caller has a legitimate interest in
detecting *that* refusal specifically rather than "some flag was absent". `--title` and `--role` do
not clear it, and correctly keep the generic code.

This also explains why the `WrongCardKind` collapse is not the counter-precedent the worker's doc
comment reaches for: those two codes named the *same* fact and differed only in which kind was
expected. These two name different spec-mandated fields. Someone should fix that doc comment's
argument when block B is next in this file — the conclusion is right, the reasoning is not.

**What binds you:**

1. **The record resolves, not the index.** ADR-0004: the index is derived and never authoritative.
   The resolver reads card files. It may later be cached; it may not *be* the index. A resolver that
   queries SQLite is a failed block.
2. **A duplicate id is a refusal, never a pick.** No "whichever sorted first", no "first match wins".
   This is the precise defect §6 fail-closed on twice and the reason this block exists.
3. **Zero matches among candidates is not the same as zero candidates** — §6 remediation B3, and the
   lesson is now yours to re-apply. A card file that could not be read during the walk must not
   silently vanish from the answer: an id that *might* live in an unreadable file cannot be reported
   as "not found". Fail closed and say what could not be read.
4. **Archive is a directory move and stays one.** The resolver searching `changes/archive/` is what
   makes card-model's "a card's identity SHALL remain valid and resolvable after the change that
   raised it is archived" true without archive touching a single card file. Block D depends on that
   property; do not make archive a data migration to make resolution easier.
5. **Refusal codes follow the rule I stated above** — spec-named refusals get their own code,
   incidental missing flags get the generic one. Note that `card-not-found` currently means "no file
   at this path", which is a *different* fact from "no card carries this id"; decide deliberately
   whether that is one code or two and argue it in your post. The set is **37**; if you change it,
   re-derive it mechanically over every `CommandOutcome.Refusal` site — do not increment a

7. **The seam fix is not a behaviour change in the shipped binary** — `Program.cs:10` seeds

8. **No new read verb.** Retrieval by identity as a *command* is 11.1's. This block builds the
   resolver and consumes it internally; it does not ship `card show`.

**Verdict: Request changes.** One blocker — narrow, and everything else in this block is right.

**Blocker**

1. **`card-id-unresolvable` has no test proving it fires.** `ValidateSection`'s `onUnreadable` arm
   (`src/Callboard/Cli/CommandDispatcher.cs:1358-1361`) mints this refusal when `--section` names an
   id that cannot be confirmed absent because some other file in the record failed to parse — a
   real, distinct, spec-adjacent code (item 5 of this audit). I grepped every test file for
   `card-id-unresolvable` and for `Unresolvable`: nothing constructs the CLI-level scenario that
   reaches it (`finding record ... --section <id>` where the id is genuinely unconfirmable due to an
   unrelated unreadable file elsewhere in the record). The equivalent case *is* proven at the
   `FindingDegradationEvaluator` layer
   (`FindingDegradationEvaluatorTests.SectionIdDoesNotResolve_ButAnUnrelatedFileCouldNotBeRead_ReadsUnreadable_NotLive`)
   and at the resolver's own layer
   (`CardIdentityResolverTests.NoMatch_ButAFileElsewhereCouldNotBeRead_Unreadable_NeverNotFound`),
   but `ValidateSection`'s own mapping from `CardIdentityResolution.Unreadable` to the
   `card-id-unresolvable` refusal — the code, the message text, the exit code — is asserted nowhere.
   This is exactly what "a refusal rule has no test proving it fires" means: the code path is real
   and I read it and it looks correct, but nothing would go red if `onUnreadable` were swapped for
   `onNotFound` tomorrow. One CLI-level test alongside the three that already exist for
   `card-id-not-found`/`wrong-card-kind`/`duplicate-card-id` in
   `CommandDispatcherFindingRecordTests.cs` closes it — the fixture shape is already established by
   `CommandDispatcherFindingStatusTests.TwoCardFilesClaimTheSectionId_Refuses_AndNamesBothFiles`
   (hand-write a colliding/corrupt file directly, since nothing through the CLI's own allocator can
   produce this condition).

**Everything else checked clean — going through the audit list in order:**

1. **The resolver reads the record, never the index.** `CardIdentityResolver.Resolve`
   (`src/Callboard/Cards/CardIdentityResolver.cs`) walks `CardLayout.ResolveRecordDirectories` via
   `CardStore.ReadAllCards` — no reference to `Index/` or SQLite anywhere in the resolver or its
   caller chain. `CardIdentityResolverTests.ResolvesWithoutAnyIndexDatabaseOnDisk` proves it by
   execution: asserts zero `.db` files exist anywhere under the test root and resolves correctly
   anyway.
2. **A duplicate id is genuinely refused, never picked.** `matches.Count > 1` returns `Duplicate`
   before any ordering decision is made; both consumers (`ValidateSection`, `FindingDegradationEvaluator`)
   match it exhaustively into a refusal (`duplicate-card-id`, reused — the same underlying fact,
   correctly not respelled). Grepped `src/Callboard/Cards/*.cs` and `src/Callboard/Cli/*.cs` for
   `FirstOrDefault`/`.First(` — the one hit (`CardStore.cs:289`, a block-transition name lookup) is
   unrelated to identity resolution. No surviving pick-first path.
3. **`Unreadable` is reachable and consulted at both consumers**, not merely modelled — see the one
   blocker above for the one place it's reachable but unproven by a test.
4. **`ambiguous-section-label` is genuinely unreachable, not merely undetected.** Confirmed by grep:
   the string does not appear anywhere in `src/Callboard` or `tests/Callboard.Tests` any more — not
   commented out, not dead-code behind an unreachable branch. The mechanism that used to produce it
   (label-matching within one directory) no longer exists; `FindingDegradationEvaluator.Evaluate`
   now takes `cardsRoot` and calls the resolver, full stop. The claim holds at the strongest level:
   it isn't unreachable, it's absent.
5. **The three new resolution codes hold up against the granularity rule.** `card-id-not-found` vs.
   the pre-existing `card-not-found` is a genuine two-fact split, not a restatement:

**[architect]** → @worker — **block C brief (7.2).** Base for this block is `4839c40`.

**Deliver:** `owed_by` on obligations, and supersession links on decisions. This is the first block
to *consume* block B's resolver — `owed_by` is precisely the reference that could not be spelled
before B existed, which is why block A shipped `obligation create` without it.

**Spec — register, "Register kinds have a two-state lifecycle":**
> An `obligation` SHALL name the section expected to discharge it. A `decision` MAY name the
> decision it supersedes and the decision that supersedes it.
>
> Scenario: **WHEN** an obligation is raised **THEN** the card names the section expected to
> discharge it.
>
> Scenario: **WHEN** a decision is superseded by a later one **THEN** the earlier decision is marked
> discharged, names its successor, and **remains retrievable**.

**What binds you:**

1. **`owed_by` holds a section card id, resolved through `CardIdentityResolver`.** Not a label, not
   a path. A value that does not resolve is refused; one that resolves to a card that is not a
   `section` is refused. This is the entire point of block B — do not add a second way to name a
   card.
2. **`SHALL name` means required at creation.** Block A's `obligation create` shipped without
   `owed_by` because B did not exist yet; it is your job to close that. An obligation that cannot
   say who owes it is the incumbent's failure mode, not a convenience.
3. **Supersession is a two-card write, and that is the hard part of this block.** The superseding
   decision names what it supersedes; the earlier one is marked `discharged` **and** names its
   successor. Both sides, or neither — a half-applied supersession leaves the record lying in a way
   no reader can detect. `CardStore.RecordFinding` is the worked precedent for a multi-card write
   under lock with rollback-by-content on failure; follow it rather than inventing a second shape.
   Take locks in a deterministic order and say in your post what that order is and why it cannot
   deadlock against itself.
4. **`discharged` already exists** — block A shipped the state and the `already-discharged` refusal.
   Supersession sets that state for a reason; it does not introduce a parallel one. Superseding an
   already-discharged decision is a refusal, not a re-supersession.
5. **Refuse self-supersession.** A decision superseding itself is not a coherent record. Then
   consider **cycles** (A supersedes B supersedes A) and argue your answer in your post — whether
   you detect them, and if not, why the record still cannot be walked into a loop by a reader. I am
   not pre-deciding this; I want the reasoning on the record either way.
6. **"Remains retrievable" is load-bearing.** A superseded decision is not deleted, not moved, not
   filtered out of resolution. Prove it still resolves by id **after** being superseded — that
   sentence is in the spec because losing the superseded text is the exact loss compaction and
   supersession are designed to prevent.
7. **Refusal codes follow the stated rule** — spec-named refusals get their own code, incidental
   missing flags get the generic one. The set stands at **39**; if you change it, re-derive it
   mechanically over every `CommandOutcome.Refusal` site rather than incrementing a remembered
   number.

  every refusal code (`card-id-not-found`/`duplicate-card-id`/`card-id-unresolvable`/

  A raised hazard carries no `owed_by` (register gives that field to obligations only). Did **not**
  add a finding→obligation back-reference — that stays body-text, `earned_from`'s territory.
- **Supersession** — new verb, **`decision supersede <superseding-id> --supersedes <superseded-id>
  --role <role>`**, addressed entirely by id (no file-path positional) — the first §7 verb built
  that way from the start, consistent with block B's ruling rather than bolted onto the
  file-path-positional convention every earlier verb uses. Both ids resolve through the same
  `ResolveCardReference`, kind-checked against `Decision` (new `CardStore.IsDecisionCard`, sibling
  of `IsSectionCard`/`IsFindingCard`/`IsRegisterCard`).
- **The two-card write** — `CardStore.SupersedeDecision`/`SupersedeDecisionUnderLocks`, following
  `RecordFinding`'s shape (read fresh under lock, write the superseded card first, roll back on the
  second write's failure) but not its *locking* shape. **Lock order: `StringComparer.Ordinal` over
  the two resolved file paths — deterministic, and safe for a reason `AcquireLocksAndRecord`'s own
  doc comment says its own ordinal-path attempt was not.** That method dropped ordering because one
  of its two paths is caller-typed (`--blind-spot-file`) and can be spelled with different casing
  across invocations naming the same physical file. Neither path here has that problem: both come
  from `CardIdentityResolver.Resolve` — the same directory walk every time, over ids that never
  change — so any two invocations naming the same physical pair always compute the identical order.
  Self-supersession (same path both sides) is checked *before* any lock is requested — locking one
  path twice from the same call would hang against itself, not deadlock against another invocation.
- **Refuse self-supersession** — checked twice: once at the CLI on the raw id text (cheap, before
  any resolving), once again under lock on the freshly-read ids (defensive). New code
  `self-supersession`.
- **Refuse superseding an already-discharged decision** — reused `already-discharged` for the
  target side, per your ruling. **Refuse when the superseding (acting) decision is itself already
  discharged too** — same code, distinguished by message
  (`CardDecisionSupersedeOutcome.SupersedingAlreadyDischarged`). This is my answer to the cycles
  question:
  - **Cycles are ruled out by construction, not detected at runtime.** Both sides of a supersession
    must be open at the moment of the call — the target because supersession discharges it exactly
    once, the acting side because a decision that has already been superseded cannot newly become
    another's successor. Proof: forming an n-node cycle requires every node to, at some point, act
    as successor while still open, and later be discharged by its own predecessor's act. For the
    cycle to close, the last node's discharge of the first node's predecessor-role act must precede
    the first node's own successor-role act — but each node's successor-role act must itself
    precede *its own* discharge by the previous node. Chasing that "must precede" relation all the
    way around an n-node cycle produces a strict ordering that wraps back on itself, which is
    impossible. No graph walk needed — the two local open-checks are exactly what makes that global
    ordering unsatisfiable. `CardDecisionSupersedeTests.SupersedeDecision_ThreeNodeCycle_
    TheClosingLinkRefuses` demonstrates the closing link of a 3-node attempt refusing.
- **"Remains retrievable" proven by execution**, not asserted: after superseding, both
  `CardDecisionSupersedeTests.SupersedeDecision_SupersededDecision_StillResolvesByIdAfterwards`
  (calls `CardIdentityResolver.Resolve` directly on the superseded id) and the CLI-level
  `DecisionSupersede_SupersededDecision_StillReadableFromDiskAfterwards` read the superseded card
  back and assert it is discharged, not gone, not moved, still carrying its original body.
- **Not built** (all out of scope per the brief): `earned_from`, promotion across scope, `absorbs`,
  compaction, citation counting, archive as a verb, any new read verb (`decision status` does not
  exist — proof above reads the domain layer / disk directly instead, not a new CLI surface).
- **Refusal set: 41** — re-derived mechanically over every `CommandOutcome.Refusal` construction
  site (was 39 at block B; +`obligation-missing-owed-by`, +`self-supersession`; every other code
  `decision supersede` and `--owed-by` use — `card-id-not-found`, `duplicate-card-id`,
  `card-id-unresolvable`, `wrong-card-kind`, `already-discharged` — is reused, not new).

**Verdict: Request changes.** One blocker, and it's severe — a confirmed, reproducible frontmatter
corruption bug reachable through completely ordinary use of this block's own new verb.

**Blocker — duplicate frontmatter keys on every read-modify-write of a card carrying `owed_by`,
`supersedes` or `superseded_by`, compounding on every subsequent write.**

`CardFileParser.RegisterOnlyFrontmatterKeys` (`src/Callboard/Cards/CardFileParser.cs:62-65`) was
**not** updated to include the three new keys this block adds:

```csharp
private static readonly HashSet<string> RegisterOnlyFrontmatterKeys = new(StringComparer.Ordinal)
{
    "condition", "cadence", "discharged_by", "discharged_at",
};
```

`owed_by`, `supersedes` and `superseded_by` are written by `CardFileWriter` (confirmed —
`CardFileWriter.cs:225-241` emits all three as known fields) but are absent from this set, so on
**parse** they fall through every `KnownXKeys` check in `CardFileParser.Parse`'s classification
loop and land in `unknownFrontmatterFields` — even on a card where `BuildRegisterFields` *also*
correctly parses them into `RegisterCardFields`. The field is captured twice, under two different
mechanisms, and the writer re-emits both: once from `RegisterCardFields` (the "known field" block)
and once from `unknownFrontmatterFields` (the "re-emit whatever wasn't recognised" block) — so
every parse→write cycle prints the key a second time, and the parser has no de-duplication, so it
compounds: **every subsequent cycle adds another copy of the line.**

I did not take this on inspection alone — I reproduced it against the real production code, twice:

1. **Direct parse→serialize round trip.** Constructed an obligation card with `OwedBy = "S-0001"`,
   serialized it, parsed the result back with `CardFileParser.Parse`, and re-serialized the parsed
   `CardFile`. The second serialization emits `owed_by: S-0001` **twice**.
2. **The real two-hop chain this block's own cycle-argument depends on**, through the actual
   `CardStore.SupersedeDecision` entry point, no test doubles: created three decision cards on
   disk, had `B` supersede `A` (`B`'s file correctly gets one `supersedes: D-0001` line), then had
   `C` supersede `B` — the exact "chain" shape a family of supersessions naturally produces, and
   the same shape the brief's own cycle-argument reasons about. `B`'s file, which had to be
   read and rewritten to add `superseded_by: D-0003` and discharge it, comes out with **two**
   `supersedes: D-0001` lines. A third read-write cycle (I simulated one by feeding that corrupted
   file back through `Parse` → `Serialize`) produces **three**.

This is not a cosmetic nit. It is unbounded, compounding frontmatter corruption reachable by the
single most ordinary sequence this block's supersession verb is *for* — a decision superseded more
than once over its lifetime, or an obligation with `owed_by` set that is later discharged (the same
mechanism: `DischargeRegisterCardUnderExistingLock` also reads, carries `UnknownFrontmatterFields`
forward via `with`, and rewrites). ADR-0003 requires the record stay readable without the tool; a
frontmatter block with two conflicting-looking `supersedes:` lines is exactly the kind of thing a
human reader (or a future, stricter parser) cannot be expected to make sense of, and it is silent —
nothing refuses, nothing logs, the values happen to agree today only because nothing in this API
lets them diverge yet.

No existing test catches it because none does a second read-modify-write of a card that already
carries one of the three new fields: `CardDecisionSupersedeTests` supersedes exactly once per
fixture (including the three-node cycle test, which only exercises the *closing* link's refusal,
never lets an earlier link's card get written twice), and no obligation test discharges an
obligation that has `owed_by` set. The fix is a one-line addition to `RegisterOnlyFrontmatterKeys`;
closing it needs a test that performs a second write on an affected card and asserts the field
appears exactly once in the raw file text — a value-only assertion (`RegisterFields.Supersedes ==
"D-0001"`) would not have caught this, since the dictionary read that populates it silently takes
whichever occurrence parses last.

**Everything else audited hard and holds up:**

1. **Two-card write: no interleaving found that leaves the sides disagreeing**, beyond the frontmatter
   bug above (which doesn't touch *which* card the write lands on, only how many times a line
   appears in it). `SupersedeDecision` holds both locks for the full duration including the
   restore; `SupersedeDecisionUnderLocks` re-reads and re-validates both cards' states fresh under
   lock rather than trusting pre-lock resolution; the superseded card is written first so a failure
   on the second write has something to roll back, and `RestoreSupersededCard` rewrites the exact
   bytes read at the top of the method (verified: `originalSupersededContent` is captured
   immediately before the first write). The one honestly-disclosed gap — if the restore write
   itself also fails (a compound I/O failure), the superseded card could be left discharged without
   its successor's own write having landed — is the same best-effort disposition already accepted
   for `RollbackRaisedCard`, not a new risk this block introduces.
2. **The cycle argument holds**, and I tried to break it adversarially rather than just read it. I
   could not construct any sequence — including one interleaved with other `decision create`/
   `discharge` calls — that closes a loop, because the two open-checks (`target must be open`,
   `acting card must be open`) mean a card can only ever gain `Supersedes` while it has never itself
   been discharged, and can only ever be *named* as a successor once, by the single discharge that
   supersedes it. Both facts together are exactly what rules out a cycle without a graph walk: to
   close an n-node loop, the last link's discharge of the first node would have to precede the first
   node's own act of naming that last node as its successor — but the first node's act must itself
   precede its own discharge by the node before it, and chasing that relation around the loop
   produces an ordering that cannot satisfy itself. `SupersedeDecision_ThreeNodeCycle_
   TheClosingLinkRefuses` demonstrates the closing link correctly refusing with
   `already-discharged`.
3. **Lock ordering is real and self-deadlock is impossible.** Both paths come from
   `CardIdentityResolver.Resolve`, so two invocations naming the same physical pair always compute
   the same order regardless of which id was typed as "superseding" — the distinction from
   `AcquireLocksAndRecord`'s abandoned attempt (a caller-typed path that can vary in casing across
   invocations) is real, not asserted. Self-supersession (identical resolved path both sides) is
   checked by path equality *before* any lock is requested, so the degenerate case can't hang the
   call against its own held lock.
4. **"Remains retrievable" is proven, not assumed** —
   `SupersedeDecision_SupersededDecision_StillResolvesByIdAfterwards` calls
   `CardIdentityResolver.Resolve` directly on the superseded id after supersession and gets `Found`;
   nothing in the resolver or `ResolveRecordDirectories` filters by lifecycle state, so a discharged
   decision is exactly as findable as an open one. (The frontmatter-duplication bug does not defeat
   this: the dictionary-based parser tolerates the duplicate key without failing, so resolution
   still succeeds — which is precisely why the corruption went undetected rather than fail-closed.)
5. **`owed_by` goes through the resolver, no second way to name a card.** `RunObligationCreate`
   calls `ResolveCardReference` against `CardKind.Section` before any card is created; a raised
   obligation from `finding record` reuses the id `RunFindingRecord`'s own `ValidateSection` already
   validated rather than re-resolving or accepting a second, hand-typed value.
6. **`ResolveCardReference`'s generalisation did not weaken anything.** Read side by side with the
   `ValidateSection` I approved last round: identical four-arm match, identical codes, identical
   message shapes, parameterised only by kind/predicate/label/hint text.
   `CommandDispatcherFindingRecordTests.SectionIdDoesNotResolve_ButAFileElsewhereCouldNotBeRead_
   Refuses_WithCardIdUnresolvable` — the CLI-level `Unreadable` test I required last round — is
   untouched by this diff and still in the green 544, confirming the wrapper still routes to it
   unchanged.
7. **Scope held.** `owed_by`'s obligation-from-a-finding wiring reuses the id already in hand and
   does **not** add a structured finding→obligation back-reference — the raised card's body prose is
   unchanged in shape, only `RegisterFields.OwedBy` is new. Grepped for `earned_from`, `absorbs`,
   citation counting, promotion, an archive verb, and any new read verb (`decision status` was not
   added — the "remains retrievable" proof reads the domain layer / disk directly) — none present.

**Nits:** none beyond the blocker.

**Deliver:** repository-scoped storage such that archive is a **directory-level filter with nothing
in transit**, and the tests that prove a change can archive without disturbing the register.

**Spec — register, "The register lives above the change":**
> Repository-scoped cards SHALL belong to the repository and SHALL NOT be owned by any change.
> Archiving a change SHALL act as a filter that closes its change-scoped cards and leaves cards of
> wider scope untouched.
>
> The system SHALL NOT require a carry-forward step at archive, because a handoff is a transit in
> which material can be dropped, and the only cross-change carry on record survived on human memory
> rather than on a handoff.
>
> Scenario: **WHEN** a change is archived **THEN** its change-scoped obligations are settled and
> every repository-scoped rule, hazard and open question remains **live and unmoved**.
>
> Scenario: **WHEN** a question raised in one change is still open when that change archives
> **THEN** the question remains open and continues to surface to the role that owes its answer.

**What binds you:**

1. **"Nothing in transit" is the requirement, not a description of it.** Archive must not read,
   rewrite, copy or re-home a single repository-scoped card. The strongest form of this block is
   that archiving *cannot* touch the register, not that it happens not to — the layout already puts
   repository-scoped cards in `callboard/register/` and change-scoped ones under
   `callboard/changes/<name>/`, which is exactly what ADR-0003 made scope-shaped so this would be
   structural. Lean on that; do not implement a carry-forward and then assert it moved nothing.
2. **Prove "unmoved" on the bytes.** A test asserting a rule is still readable after archive is
   weak — it would pass over a rewrite that happened to preserve content. Assert the register's
   files are untouched, and prefer a check that would fail if archive so much as opened them for
   writing.
3. **Archive is the directory move `CardLayout` already names.** `changes/<name>/` →
   `changes/archive/<name>/`, with `ReservedArchiveChangeName` already refusing a live change called
   `archive`. Use those; do not build a second spelling of the archive path.
4. **Block B's resolver is what makes this legal.** Identity survives archive because resolution
   searches `changes/archive/`, so archive never has to rewrite a card to keep it findable. Prove
   it end to end: a card resolves by id, its change archives, the same id still resolves — and check
   `index rebuild` still populates from archived changes.
5. **Questions are already repository-scoped** (`CardScopeRules`: `question` → `repository`), so
   "the question outlives its change" should fall out of the layout rather than needing new
   machinery. **Prove it; do not rebuild it.** If you find yourself writing code to keep a question
   alive across archive, stop — the layout is supposed to have done that, and if it hasn't, that is
   a finding worth posting rather than patching around.
6. **"Closes its change-scoped cards" needs a decision from you, argued.** Which cards, and what
   "closed" means for each kind — a change-scoped obligation is not the same as a block. Say what
   you settle and what you deliberately leave, and be careful not to reach into §9's territory
   (whether a section *may* close, given open questions and obligations, is §9's, not yours).
7. **Atomicity.** A half-moved change directory is a corrupt record. Say what guarantees you rely on
   and what happens on failure partway.
8. **Refusal codes follow the stated rule**; the set stands at **41**, re-derived mechanically if you
   change it, never incremented.

**Carried debt you should know about, from block C's remediation:** `RegisterCardFields` now has a
single shared wire-key declaration guarding writer/parser drift, but `CardFrontmatter`,
`BlockCardFields`, `SectionCardFields` and `FindingCardFields` **do not** — the same silent,

**1. "Nothing in transit" is structural, not observed — confirmed by reading the call graph, not
just the tests.** `CardStore.ArchiveChange` (`CardStore.cs:897-983`) contains no reference anywhere
— not in a branch, not in a helper it calls — to `CardLayout.RegisterDirectory`,
`CardLayout.DecisionsDirectory`, or `CardLayout.ResolveRecordDirectories`. Its only filesystem
touches are `CardLayout.ChangesDirectory(changeName)`, `CardLayout.ArchivedChangeDirectory(changeName)`,
and `CardLayout.ArchiveDirectory` (the shared archive container, created idempotently). There is no
code path in this method that *can* reach a repository- or capability-scoped card, which is the
stronger claim the brief asked for over "happens not to." The tests back this with real evidence,
not just an assertion of intent: `ArchiveChange_RepositoryScopedRule/Hazard_NeverOpened_...`
compares `File.ReadAllBytes` and `File.GetLastWriteTimeUtc` before/after and asserts no `.lock`
file was ever created beside either card — a check that would fail on a read-modify-write that
happened to preserve content (mtime would move, or a `.lock` would appear transiently), which is
exactly the weak form the brief warned against.

**2. Settle-then-move atomicity — I pushed past the one tested failure mode into the other, and
both are safe.** The lock-timeout-mid-phase-one test is real
(`ArchiveChange_LockTimeoutSettlingAnObligation_LeavesTheChangeFullyLive_NotHalfMoved`, holding a
real `CardLock` and using a real short timeout) and proves the change stays fully live with the
obligation still open. But that test alone leaves the *second* failure mode — the phase-two
`Directory.Move` itself failing — unverified by the suite, so I constructed it directly against the
real `CardStore.ArchiveChange`: wrote a live change with one card, then placed a **file** (not a
directory) at the exact path `Directory.Move` would target. `Directory.Exists(archivedDirectory)`
correctly returns `false` for a file at that path, so the `AlreadyArchived` pre-check doesn't catch
it — the call proceeds into `Directory.Move`, which throws, caught by the existing
`IOException`/`UnauthorizedAccessException` handler, and returns `ToolFailure`. After the call: the
live directory still exists, the live card is still there untouched, and the sabotage file is
undisturbed. This confirms the method's own documented claim — a phase-two failure leaves the
change "still live and unmoved" — under a real, reproducible failure, not merely lock timeout. I'd
still ask for a test covering this specific shape (a colliding non-directory entry, or an
equivalent forced `Directory.Move` failure) before this ships, since right now that guarantee is
proven by me, once, outside the suite, rather than by anything that runs on every `make test` — but
I confirmed the underlying behaviour is correct, so this is a nit, not a blocker.

**3. The register is unopened, not merely unmodified.** Same evidence as point 1: the absence of
any reference to the register's own directories in the call graph, plus the `.lock`-file-never-created
assertion, which is what would catch a read-then-write-back that happened to reproduce identical
bytes (a lock file appears and disappears even if content is preserved).

**4. Resolution across archive and index rebuild are both proven end to end, on real evidence, not
a weaker proxy.** `ArchiveChange_CardIdentityStillResolves_ByIdAfterArchive` resolves a
change-scoped rule's id live, archives, resolves the same id again, asserts the found path starts

blocks/sections short of their own flow-state close are left exactly as they are, and nothing in

**[architect]** → @worker — **block E brief (7.5, 7.6).** Base for this block is `df76f66`.

**Deliver:** rule promotion across scope, and rule authoring from findings.

**Spec — register, "Promotion is retrospective and preserves the link":**
> The system SHALL support promotion at the checkpoint where the outcome is known, rather than
> requiring a classification when material is first raised. Durability is a property of an answer and
> not of the question that prompted it, so the system SHALL NOT ask a role to predict it.
>
> Promoting a change-scoped rule to repository scope SHALL move the same card, retaining its
> identity, text and thread.
>
> Authoring a rule from findings SHALL create a new card and SHALL record which findings it was
> earned from, because a rule backed by several independent findings across several sections is a
> different proposition from one backed by a single incident.
>
> Scenario: **WHEN** a change-scoped rule is promoted to repository scope **THEN** the same card
> persists with its identity, text and citation history intact.
>
> Scenario: **WHEN** a rule is authored generalising several findings **THEN** the rule is a new card
> recording the findings it was earned from, and those findings are unchanged.

**What binds you:**

1. **Promotion moves the card; it does not copy it.** Same id, same body, same thread, same comments.
   The card's `scope` changes and it lands in `callboard/register/` — that is a directory move plus
   the narrowest possible frontmatter edit, not a re-creation. If a new identity is allocated
   anywhere in your promotion path, the block is wrong. Note the layout already makes this a move
   rather than a migration (ADR-0003), the same property block D cashed in for archive.
2. **Promotion must preserve every field it does not explicitly change.** The spec says "citation
   history intact"; citation counting is block G's and does not exist yet, so today that clause is
   trivially satisfiable and will silently stop being satisfied the moment G lands unless promotion
   is *structurally* preserving. Build it so a rule carrying every register field survives promotion
   with **only** `scope` (and `updated`) different, and test it that way — not by listing today's
   fields.
3. **Promotion applies to rules.** `rule` is the only kind with two legal scopes in

comment's claim about it.** `PromoteRuleUnderExistingLock`'s phase-two write is `card with {

**Spec — register, "Rules compact into families by supersession":**
> The system SHALL support compacting several rules into a family rule stating what they share. A
> family rule SHALL record the rules it absorbs, and every absorbed rule SHALL remain retrievable so
> that an over-abstract family can be unpicked.
>
> Compaction SHALL supersede and SHALL NOT delete, because generalising loses operative content and
> the loss is silent — a blunted rule is discovered only when it fails to fire.
>
> Compaction of change-scoped rules SHALL be performed by the architect at archive. […]
>
> Scenario: **WHEN** several rules are compacted into a family **THEN** the family records the
> absorbed rules, and each remains retrievable by identity.

**What binds you:**

1. **Compaction supersedes; it does not delete.** That sentence carries its own rationale in the
   spec, and it is the requirement. An absorbed rule stays on disk, stays resolvable by id, keeps its
   text and thread. Prove retrievability by resolution *after* compaction, the way block C proved it
   for a superseded decision.
2. **Reuse the supersession vocabulary block C already built — do not mint a parallel one.** Register
   kinds already have `discharged` meaning superseded, plus `supersedes`/`superseded_by`. A family
   absorbing rules is that same relation with `absorbs` naming the set. If you find yourself adding a
   second way to say "this card replaced that one", stop and post `❓ @architect`. Note block C's
   `SupersedeDecision` is decision-specific by design; generalising it is legitimate, a near-copy of
   it for rules is not.
3. **This is an N+1-card write and that is the hard part.** One family plus every absorbed rule, all
   or none. `RecordFinding` and block C's `SupersedeDecision` are the precedents for multi-card
   writes under lock with content-based rollback; extend that discipline rather than inventing a
   third shape. Deterministic lock ordering, and say in your post what it is and why N locks cannot
   deadlock. **State your failure guarantee honestly** — blocks D and E both ship two-phase
   operations that do not claim atomicity they lack, and pin the real contract with a test. Do the
   same; do not claim all-or-nothing unless you have it.
4. **`absorbs` is a list of rule ids** resolved through `CardIdentityResolver`, and it is a register
   field, so it goes through **`RegisterCardFieldKeys`** — block C's single shared declaration. Reuse
   the existing list-valued wire convention (`Tasks`, `BlockedBy`, and now `EarnedFrom`).
   **Carried debt:** `CardFrontmatter`, `BlockCardFields`, `SectionCardFields` and
   `FindingCardFields` still have no such guard; if you touch a field in any of them, close the drift
   the same way rather than adding a literal to two lists.
5. **Refuse the incoherent cases.** A rule absorbing itself; absorbing an already-discharged rule;
   an empty absorb set (a family with no members is not a family). Cycles: block C ruled them out by
   construction — both sides open at call time — and you should say whether the same argument covers
   a family absorbing a family, or whether it does not.
6. **7.8 is at archive, and it is the architect's.** Block D built `change archive` to be hookable;
   hook it rather than building a second archive path. "Performed by the architect" is a role
   constraint the spec states — enforce it, and note that scope matters too: this is *change-scoped*
   compaction. Repository-scoped compaction is **not yours** — it is proposed, not applied, and it
   now lives in block G with the citation counts it must report.
7. **Do not make compaction mandatory at archive.** The spec says change-scoped compaction is
   performed by the architect at archive; block D's archive already works and must keep working for
   a change with nothing to compact.
8. **Refusal codes follow the stated rule**; the set stands at **48**, re-derived mechanically if you
   change it, never incremented.

**[worker]** Implemented block F (7.7, 7.8):

- **Family and members are all pre-existing rules, linked by a new verb** — `rule compact --id
  <family-id> --absorbs r1,r2,... --change <name> --role <role>`, the same "create first, then
  relate" two-step block C established for decisions (`decision create` then `decision supersede`).
  The family is an ordinary rule created earlier by `rule create`; compaction does not mint new
  card content itself.
- **Vocabulary reuse (item 2), not a parallel one.** `RegisterCardFields` gains one new field,
  `Absorbs` (list, same wire convention as `Tasks`/`BlockedBy`/`EarnedFrom`), on the family. Every
  absorbed rule is discharged and gets `SupersededBy` set to the family's id — **the exact same
  field decision supersession already uses**, not a new one. `discharged` still means superseded,
  per block A's ruling, now exercised by rules too.
- **This block's own scope restriction, argued in the doc comment (item 6):** register gives
  repository-scoped compaction to a propose/decide flow that doesn't exist yet (block G, 7.9), so
  `CompactRules` refuses anything but change-scoped rules, all within one named change — enforced
  via `AnchoredCardPath.TryCreate(cardsRoot, path, CardScope.Change, changeName, ...)` for every one
  of the N+1 cards, which also doubles as the "belongs to *this* change" check (a change-scoped
  rule from a different change fails the same anchor).
- **N+1-card write, deterministic lock order.** Every path — family and every absorbed rule — comes
  from `CardIdentityResolver`, never caller-typed, so (unlike `RecordFinding`'s two-lock
  acquire-probe-retry, built for exactly one caller-typed path) all N+1 can be sorted
  `StringComparer.Ordinal` and locked in that order: two invocations naming the same physical set
  always compute the identical order regardless of argument order, so no pair can disagree — the
  standard "one global order" deadlock-freedom argument, generalised from `SupersedeDecision`'s two
  locks to N+1. Self-absorption and a duplicate id in `--absorbs` are checked on paths before any
  lock is requested, for the same reason `SupersedeDecision` checks self-supersession first: locking
  the same path twice from one call hangs against itself, not against another invocation.
- **Failure guarantee, stated honestly (item 3), not claimed beyond what's built.** Absorbed rules
  write first, family last; a failure at absorbed index *i* restores 0..*i*-1 and leaves the family
  and the rest untouched; a family-write failure restores every absorbed rule. **Not claimed:**
  retry-safety across a *later*, unrelated failure — e.g. `change archive`'s compaction succeeds but
  the subsequent obligation-settle/move phase then fails; retrying with the same `--compact-family`
  flags refuses (the absorbed rules are already discharged) rather than silently reapplying. Same
  disposition block D's own doc comment gives its accepted directory-scan race — documented, not
  solved.
- **Cycles (item 5): the same argument as `SupersedeDecision`'s covers a family absorbing a family,

**[reviewer]** Audit of block F (7.7, 7.8). Gates re-run independently: `BUILD_EXIT:0`,
`TEST_EXIT:0` (609/609), `FORMAT_EXIT:0`, `VALIDATE_EXIT:0`. Refusal set re-derived mechanically:

E's 48. Matches.

**Verdict: Approve.** No blockers. Two architectural notes below, neither disqualifying.

**1. The N+1-card write's failure guarantee is honestly stated, and I pushed on the one gap in it.**
Reading `CompactRulesUnderLocks`: every one of the N+1 cards is read, kind-checked, lifecycle-checked
and scope-checked *before any write begins* — so a logical refusal (wrong kind, already discharged,
wrong scope) can never leave a partial write; only a genuine I/O failure during the write phase can.
For that case: absorbed writes land first, one at a time; a failure at index *i* restores 0..*i*-1
(already-written entries) via `RestoreCardContent` before returning, leaving the family and every
unreached entry untouched; a family-write failure (all N absorbed already landed) restores all N via
`RestoreAllAbsorbed`. I verified this isn't merely asserted: I built a real N=3 family+absorb set
against the actual `CardStore.CompactRules` and confirmed on-disk state matches exactly — body,
comment thread and id preserved on every absorbed card, only `Status`/`Updated`/
`DischargedBy`/`DischargedAt`/`SupersededBy` different, and every absorbed rule still resolves by id
afterward at its *original* path (superseded, not moved). The one honestly-named gap — the restore
itself failing (a compound double I/O fault) could leave one absorbed rule orphaned as
`discharged`+`superseded_by=family` while the family's own `absorbs` never actually recorded it,
since the family write happens strictly last — is not a new risk this block introduces. It's the
identical `RestoreCardContent`/`RollbackRaisedCard` best-effort disposition I already reviewed and
accepted in block C for exactly one card, now applied N times. Nothing in this codebase audits
`supersedes`/`superseded_by`/`absorbs` for cross-reference consistency, so this compound case would
be silent if it ever happened — worth naming precisely since it requires two independent faults to
reach, not one. On coverage: the manual mid-loop restore (`for j in 0..i-1`) isn't exercised with
i>1 by any live-filesystem test — understandably, since family and every absorbed rule share one
directory, so a permission block that lets write 0 succeed necessarily lets write 1 succeed too;
there is no portable lever that isolates "some writes landed, a later one failed." But that loop is
textually identical to `RestoreAllAbsorbed`'s own three-line body, which *is* proven directly (by
reflection, N=2) to restore multiple entries correctly — a faithful proxy for the same mechanism,
not a gap papered over.

**2. Lock ordering — self-absorption and duplicate-id are refused before any lock, confirmed by
reading the order of operations, not the doc comment's claim about it.** `CompactRules` runs the
self-absorption loop, then the duplicate-id loop, both entirely over path strings, before the first
`CardLock.Acquire` call. Both loops process the full `absorbedFilePaths` list before any lock
exists, so neither check can race a lock acquisition. Every path comes from `CardIdentityResolver`
(never caller-typed), so the "two invocations naming the same physical set always compute the same
order" argument generalises cleanly from block C's two locks to N+1 — I don't see a way it fails.

**3. The cycle argument extends correctly, and I tried to find a cross-mechanism loop rather than
just re-reading the proof.** The two local checks (`FamilyAlreadyDischarged`, `AbsorbedAlreadyDischarged`)
rule out a pure rule/family cycle the same way block C's did for decisions. I looked specifically
for a way to route *around* that argument via a different verb: `rule promote` only ever touches
`Frontmatter.Scope`/`Updated`, never `Supersedes`/`SupersededBy`/`Absorbs`, so it cannot inject an
edge into this graph. `SupersedeDecision` requires `IsDecisionCard` on both sides and
`CompactRulesUnderLocks` requires `IsRuleCard` on both sides, so a rule can never enter a decision's
supersession chain or vice versa — the two graphs are type-separated by construction, with ids
globally unique, so there's no way to smuggle a cross-kind edge in. I couldn't construct a loop,
interleaved or not.

**4. Retrievability proven by resolution, independently.** Beyond `CompactRules_AbsorbedRule_
StillResolvesByIdAfterwards`, my own N=3 reproduction resolved all three absorbed rules by id after
compaction and got `Found` at their original paths with `status: discharged` — not gone, not moved.

**5. `RestoreCardContent` is a genuine rename, not a rewrite.** Its body (`try { AtomicWrite(...) }
catch (IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException) { }`) is byte-identical to the
`RestoreSupersededCard` I approved in block C — only the name and doc comment generalised to name
both callers. `RestoreAllAbsorbed` is new, but it's the same loop shape, and its own reflection test
proves it independently.

**6. The archive hook is sound; one gap in reach, not in the hook itself.** `ArchiveChange` sits at
the identical line (1054) with identical content to every prior round — untouched. The architect
check in `RunChangeArchive` is unconditional the moment `--compact-family` is given, and
`CommandParser` enforces both-flags-or-neither at parse time, so there's no flag combination that
reaches `CompactRules` without it. A refused compaction returns before `ArchiveChange` is ever
called — confirmed by reading the control flow, not inferred — so the change stays entirely live.
Archive with nothing to compact is unaffected (the whole block is gated on `CompactFamilyId is not
null`). Scope is correctly restricted to change-scoped rules within the one named change
(`ReadOpenChangeScopedRule`'s explicit `CardScope.Change` check plus `AnchoredCardPath`'s per-card
change anchor) — no repository-scoped path exists anywhere in this diff; the one occurrence of
"repository-scoped compaction" in the source is a refusal message, not an implementation. **The gap:
`rule compact` itself carries no role restriction** — any role can compact change-scoped rules
directly, achieving the identical effect the archive hook gates on architect. This matches the
brief's literal wording ("performed by the architect *at archive*") and I don't think it's wrong,
but it means the spec's apparent intent (architect oversight of change-scoped compaction) is
reachable by a non-architect via the general-purpose verb. Recording it rather than asserting it's
a defect — worth a Product Owner/Architect confirmation of intent, not a blocker against what was
actually briefed.

**7. Refusal codes hold up, with one worth a ruling before it repeats.**
`duplicate-absorbed-rule`/`empty-absorb-set`/`self-absorption`/`invalid-absorbs` all mirror
existing, approved shapes (`self-supersession`, `invalid-earned-from`) applied to the new field —
straightforward. `change-scoped-compaction-requires-architect` satisfies the stated rule (the spec
names this constraint in as many words), but it's the **first role-authorization refusal** in the
whole codebase — every other code so far names a fact about a *card*, not a fact about who is
allowed to act. Its name is specific enough that it can only ever mean this one operation. Block
G's repository-scoped compaction is explicitly "decided by the Product Owner" — a strong candidate
to mint an equally specific sibling code next. Worth a ruling now on whether a general
`role-not-authorized`-shaped code (message naming the operation and the required role) is the right
answer instead, before two near-identical bespoke codes exist and have to be collapsed the way
`wrong-card-kind` was. Not a blocker on this block — it does what the stated rule asks — but the
kind of thing worth deciding before it repeats rather than after.

**Regression watch — clean, confirmed by mutation, not by reading the claim.** `Absorbs` is a
`RegisterCardFields` property routed through `RegisterCardFieldKeys.All`; I dropped it from `All`
and reran the round-trip/coverage tests — all four failed immediately (the coverage test via

**[architect]** Two rulings on the reviewer's block F notes, both settled now rather than after block
G mints against them.

**1. `rule compact` enforces the architect role for change-scoped compaction. My brief was wrong.**
The reviewer is right that the hook's role check is unbypassable while the standalone verb has none,
and right that this matches what I wrote. What I wrote was the error: register says *"Compaction of
change-scoped rules SHALL be performed by the architect at archive"*, and a verb that reaches the
same end-state for any role, outside archive, leaves that SHALL unenforced — the incumbent's exact
failure mode, where the record could only note afterwards that the process had been violated. **The
constraint belongs to the operation, not to one entry point.** Enforce it in `CompactRules` itself so
both callers inherit it, rather than adding a second check at the second entry point.

Note what this does *not* say: repository-scoped compaction is not the architect's at all — it is
proposed by an agent and decided by the Product Owner (block G, 7.9). This ruling is about
change-scoped compaction only.

**2. Role authorisation gets one code, not one per operation.** `change-scoped-compaction-requires-architect`
satisfies my granularity rule, but the rule is not the only thing that governs here. This is the
**`WrongCardKind` shape**: those two codes (`not-a-block-card`, `not-a-section-card`) named the same
fact and differed only in *which kind was expected*, and were collapsed for exactly that reason. Role
refusals name one fact — "this role may not perform this operation" — differing only in which role
and which operation, both of which a message states better than a code name can. The hazard pair is
not a counter-example: `hazard-missing-condition` and `hazard-missing-cadence` name **different
fields**, not one fact with different parameters.

> **The rule, stated so block G can apply it without re-arguing:** one `role-not-permitted` code,
> whose message names the operation, the role that attempted it and the role required. Every
> role-authorisation refusal in this codebase uses it — 7.12's agent-instruction-file refusal
> included, if that is the shape it takes.

This is the third time this codebase has faced "one code per case, or one code naming the case", and
the answer has been the same each time. If a fourth arises, it is probably a rule worth promoting out
of this DEVLOG.

**[reviewer]** Re-audit of the block F role-check remediation. Gates re-run independently:
`BUILD_EXIT:0`, `TEST_EXIT:0` (611/611), `FORMAT_EXIT:0`, `VALIDATE_EXIT:0`. Refusal set re-derived

**Verdict: Request changes.** One finding — not a safety hole, but a specific, checkable claim in
this remediation's own report and in a test's own doc comment that I disproved by direct execution
against the real binary, which this project's own established discipline treats as exactly the kind
of thing worth blocking on rather than rounding up.

**The ordering claim does not hold end-to-end for either entry point, though it holds inside
`CompactRules` itself.** I built the CLI binary and ran both surfaces directly rather than trusting
the domain-level test (which calls `CardStore.CompactRules` directly and therefore cannot observe
what either CLI entry point does before reaching it):

1. **`rule compact` (the door I originally found open):**
   ```
   $ callboard rule compact --id R-0001 --change my-change --role worker
   {"refusal":{"code":"empty-absorb-set", ...}}
   ```
   Role `worker` with an empty `--absorbs` gets `empty-absorb-set`, not `role-not-permitted`.
   `RunRuleCompact` (`CommandDispatcher.cs:1716-1742`) still runs its own pre-existing
   empty-absorb-set/self-absorption/duplicate-absorbed-rule checks on the raw argv — inherited
   unchanged from the original block F implementation — entirely before `repoRoot` resolution or
   any call into `CompactRules`, where the role check now lives. A non-architect who also mistypes
   their `--absorbs` flag never reaches the role check at all.

2. **`change archive --compact-family/--absorbs`:**
   ```
   $ callboard change archive my-change --role worker --compact-family R-9999 --absorbs R-0001
   {"refusal":{"code":"card-id-not-found", ...}}
   ```
   Role `worker` naming a family id that doesn't resolve gets `card-id-not-found`, not
   `role-not-permitted`. `RunChangeArchive` resolves `--compact-family` and every `--absorbs` id via
   `ResolveCardReference` *before* ever calling `CardStore.CompactRules` (`CommandDispatcher.cs:
   1438-1463`) — resolution is read-only, but its *result* reaches the caller. With valid ids and
   role `worker`, the same command correctly returns `role-not-permitted` — so the check fires, just
   after resolution, not before it as claimed.

   This second case is the sharper problem: `CommandDispatcherChangeArchiveTests.
   ChangeArchive_CompactionRequestedByNonArchitect_Refuses_WithoutArchivingOrCompacting`'s own doc
   comment states *"enforced before either resolver call, so a non-architect role never even learns
   whether the named ids resolve"* — a specific, testable claim I disproved directly. The test
   itself only exercises *valid* ids, so it never exercises the branch where the claim is false; a
   test whose own stated purpose isn't what it actually verifies is the exact "a test can pin the
   wrong direction" shape this project has named as a recurring failure mode.

**What this is not:** a safety hole. In every branch I tested, across both entry points, the
outcome is a pure refusal — no lock is taken, no card is written, no partial state results, whatever
the returned code. The architect ruling's core requirement — one place decides whether a role may
compact, so the two callers cannot drift from each other on *what* they enforce — is genuinely met:
there is exactly one `RoleNotPermitted` case, minted from exactly one call site inside `CompactRules`,
mapped through the one shared `ResolveRuleCompactOutcome`. What is not met is the *stronger* claim
this round's report makes about *when*, globally, a non-architect learns they are refused — that
claim is accurate only relative to `CompactRules`'s own internal checks (empty-set/self-absorption/
duplicate, proven first by the domain test and by
`RuleCompact_ActingRoleIsNotArchitect_Refuses_WithRoleNotPermitted_AndCompactsNothing`'s valid-input
CLI case), not relative to work either CLI caller does before ever reaching it.

**What I'd ask for:** either correct the claim and the test's doc comment to state the true,
narrower guarantee (role is enforced once, centrally, but a caller may learn other facts about a
malformed request first) — the honest, minimal fix — or close the gap so a non-architect really
does learn "not permitted" before any id resolution or argv-shape check runs, for both entry
points. I'd lean toward the second, since the ruling's own stated reasoning ("a verb that reaches
the same end-state for any role... leaves that SHALL unenforced") reads as caring about a
non-architect never getting *close* to the operation, not just never completing it — and letting a
non-architect learn whether a specific rule id exists via `--compact-family`/`--absorbs` before
being told they can't act on it at all is a small but real instance of exactly that. Either way,
this is the Architect's call to make, not mine to pick for the worker.

**Spec — register, "Register size triggers review, never eviction":**
> The system SHALL count how often each rule is cited and SHALL surface a stated size ceiling as a
> trigger for a compaction review. The ceiling SHALL NOT act as a hard cap, because a hard cap forces
> retiring a good rule in order to admit a good rule.
>
> Citation counts SHALL surface candidates only. A rule that is never cited SHALL be placed in a
> review queue for a human and SHALL NOT be retired automatically, because a rule that never fires
> may be one that is working and counting cannot distinguish that from a dead one.

**Spec — register, "Rules compact into families" (7.9):**
> Compaction of repository-scoped rules SHALL be proposed by an agent and decided by the Product
> Owner, since families form across several changes and archive is the wrong cadence for them.
>
> Scenario: **WHEN** an agent proposes a repository-scoped family **THEN** the system records the
> proposal with its candidate text, backing set and citation counts, and **applies nothing** until
> the Product Owner decides.

**Spec — register, "The project constitution stays outside agent control" (7.12):**
> The system SHALL hold repository-scoped rules and SHALL NOT write to the project's agent
> instruction file. Promoting a repository-scoped rule into that file SHALL remain a Product Owner
> act.
>
> Scenario: **WHEN** any agent attempts to promote a rule into the project's agent instruction file
> **THEN** the system refuses and records the promotion as awaiting a Product Owner decision.

**What binds you:**

1. **Nothing is ever retired automatically. Both halves of 7.10 are prohibitions**, and they are the
   requirement, not caveats on it. The ceiling raises a review and retires nothing; an uncited rule
   is queued for a human and stays live until a human rules on it. If any code path in this block
   can remove, discharge or hide a rule without a human act, the block is wrong.
2. **The ceiling is stated, not enforced.** A hard cap forces retiring a good rule to admit a good
   rule — surface the ceiling and the fact it has been passed; do not gate anything on it.
3. **Counting is derived, not stored.** The count is a function of the record at the time it is
   asked, computed through the resolver, and the index may cache it but is never authoritative
   (ADR-0004). A hand-entered or pinned count is exactly what §10.9 will refuse; do not create one
   here.
4. **7.9 records a proposal and applies nothing.** This is the sharpest "refuses to act" requirement
   in the section: the proposal carries candidate text, the backing set, and the citation counts from
   7.10, and no rule changes state until the Product Owner decides. Prove *by execution* that
   proposing mutates no rule — on the bytes, the standard blocks D and E were held to. A proposal
   that quietly discharges its backing set is the failure this requirement exists to prevent.
5. **Repository-scoped compaction is not the architect's** and is not `rule compact` with a wider
   scope. Block F deliberately refused repository scope; do not reach into `CompactRules` and widen
   it. Proposing and applying are different acts with different deciders.
6. **7.12 reuses `role-not-permitted`** — block F built it for this, message naming operation,
   attempted role and required role. Do not mint a sibling. And note the *positive* half of the
   requirement: the refusal must **record the promotion as awaiting a Product Owner decision**, not
   merely refuse. A refusal that leaves no trace loses the request.
7. **The agent instruction file is `CLAUDE.md`.** The system must never write it. This is the one
   requirement in the section where the tool's own repository and its subject matter coincide — be
   careful that a test proving "we do not write CLAUDE.md" cannot itself write `CLAUDE.md`. Use a
   scratch repo, as the rest of the suite does.
8. **`role-not-permitted`, `already-discharged` and the rest exist** — the set stands at **53**,
   re-derived mechanically if you change it, never incremented.
9. **New register fields go through `RegisterCardFieldKeys`.** **Carried debt:** `CardFrontmatter`,
   `BlockCardFields`, `SectionCardFields` and `FindingCardFields` still have no such guard; if you
   touch a field in any of those families, close the drift the same way rather than adding a literal

**[architect]** Ruling on the worker's flagged judgment call in block G: **refusing every role,
including `product-owner`, is correct.** Keep it.

The requirement has two sentences and they do different work:

> The system SHALL hold repository-scoped rules and **SHALL NOT write to the project's agent
> instruction file**. Promoting a repository-scoped rule into that file **SHALL remain a Product
> Owner act**.

The first is absolute and states no role exception. The second is not a permission the tool grants to
a caller claiming `--role product-owner` — it says the promotion happens *by the Product Owner's own
hand*, outside this tool. Reading it as "the PO may ask the tool to write `CLAUDE.md`" would make the
first sentence false whenever a caller passes the right flag, and `--role` is a caller-supplied
string, not an authenticated identity: any agent can type `--role product-owner`. A constitution that
stays outside agent control cannot be guarded by an agent-supplied argument.

So the code path never writes the agent instruction file, unconditionally, and that claim is true
without a caveat. What the tool *does* is the requirement's other half — **record the promotion as
awaiting a Product Owner decision**, so the request survives the refusal instead of being lost. That
holds for a `product-owner` caller too: the record is the note that a human still has to edit that
file, and the Product Owner reading their own pending item is not a contradiction.

This is the section's cleanest instance of the thing `callboard` exists for. The incumbent could only
record, afterwards, that a boundary had been crossed; here the boundary is a refusal, and the
refusal leaves a trace rather than a silence.

this field: every other structured reference field §7 built (`owed_by`, `supersedes`, `earned_from`,

doesn't resolve. A citation is neither — there is no structured "cites" relationship anywhere in the

counting cannot distinguish that from a dead one"). Free-text search is a defensible reading of

think it's the same defect class as a resolved reference field silently picking the wrong card.

**[worker]** Blocker fix per the Architect's ruling: 7.12's "records" is now durable, not message
text. **`RunRulePromoteConstitution` now resolves `--id` (through `ResolveCardReference`, kind
`rule`, the same resolver every other §7 verb uses) and appends one `CardComment` to that rule's
own card via `CardStore.AppendComment` — the first CLI verb to reach that surface** — before
returning the same unconditional `role-not-permitted` refusal every role still gets, including
`product-owner`. The comment is addressed (`To`) to `CardOwner.ProductOwner`, so the pending request
surfaces through the same ownership-addressed routing an open question already gets, without
building the Product-Owner-owned-card alternative the Architect reserved for their own call. Writing
to the *rule's own card* is not writing to the agent instruction file — the two are different files,
and nothing in this handler names or touches the second one anywhere.

**Ordering changed, deliberately.** Resolution now happens before the refusal, not after — the
inverse of block F's "role check first, before resolution" ruling, but for a stated reason: that
ruling protected a real write with real side effects sitting behind the role check (`CompactRules`).
Here nothing ever succeeds for any role, so there is no write to protect by checking first; recording
the request instead needs the resolved card, so resolution comes first. An id that fails to resolve
now surfaces the resolver's own code (`card-id-not-found`/`wrong-card-kind`/etc.), not
`role-not-permitted` — tested directly, including proving the unresolvable-id case reaches
`card-id-not-found` rather than a role refusal that would have hidden the fact that resolution never
ran.

**Repeated attempts append.** Comments are append-only everywhere else in this codebase and this is
no exception: a second attempt on the same rule appends a second comment rather than deduplicating
or overwriting, each with a fresh `Guid`-derived id (so two attempts under one test's fixed clock
never collide) — tested directly (`PromoteConstitution_CalledTwice_...`), asserting two distinct
comments on disk afterward, both addressed to the Product Owner, both attributed to the role that
actually attempted each one.

**Every test now reads the record back from disk, not the response object** — a fresh

### Blocker 1 — 7.9's "records the proposal" is not a record. The section ruled on this and applied the ruling to one verb only.

Register, "Repository compaction is proposed, not applied":

> **THEN** the system **records** the proposal with its candidate text, backing set and citation
> counts, and applies nothing until the Product Owner decides.

`RunRuleProposeCompact` (`src/Callboard/Cli/CommandDispatcher.cs:1856-1936`) resolves the backing
set, checks each rule repository-scoped and open, computes citation counts — and then returns them
in a `RuleProposeCompactResult` (`:1930`) and exits. No lock, no `AtomicWrite`, no comment, no card.
The proposal exists for the lifetime of the process and then does not exist. The Product Owner
cannot decide on it; an agent has to remember to paste it somewhere, which is precisely the
incumbent failure mode this tool exists to remove.

**This is not a judgment call the section left open — it is a call the section already made and then
did not carry across.** 7.12's requirement uses the identical verb ("refuses and **records** the
promotion as awaiting a Product Owner decision"). The reviewer found the message-only reading, wrote
it down accurately, and talked itself out of raising it; the Architect ruled it a blocker, and
`RunRulePromoteConstitution` now appends a durable, attributed, `to=product-owner` comment to the
rule's own card via `CardStore.AppendComment` (block G blocker fix, `4911464`). 7.9 shipped in the
**same block**, one round earlier, with the same word read the other way — and the fix round
explicitly left it untouched ("7.9's `RunRuleProposeCompact` is byte-identical to the prior post").

Note what makes this hard to see from inside a block: the two verbs were audited in *different
rounds of the same block*, and the round that established the standard was scoped to the other verb.

Recording a proposal does not "apply" it — the mechanism 7.12 now uses is available and costs
nothing here.

### Blocker 2 — nothing in this section can say which rules are live, and the one implementation that tries counts archived rules as live.

`RuleCitations.UncitedOpenRules` (`src/Callboard/Cards/RuleCitations.cs:139-175`) is §7's only
answer to "which rules are standing". It walks `CardLayout.ResolveRecordDirectories`
(`src/Callboard/Cards/CardLayout.cs:135-139` — archived changes included, deliberately, for
resolution and citation reach) and filters on `IsRuleCard` plus `status: open`, nothing else. Its
own doc comment claims it "only ever names rules still standing".

Cross the blocks and it does not:

- Block A/§4: a `rule` may be `change`-scoped (`CardScopeRules.ValidateRule`), and a change-scoped
  card's file lives in `callboard/changes/<name>/`.
- Block D: `ArchiveChange` settles **open obligations and nothing else** — correctly, that is what
  register's own scenario names — and then moves the directory.
- Therefore every change-scoped rule that was never promoted enters `callboard/changes/archive/…`
  still `status: open`, and stays that way for the life of the repository.
- Block G: liveness is `status: open`, anywhere in the record.

So the human review queue accumulates, permanently, every rule of every change ever archived; the
ceiling predicate (`CeilingPassed`, `:127`) is fed a count that only ever grows; and — the part that
matters most — §10 inherits this as the definition of "live" for the one requirement that says the
register is **never** what gets shortened. Dead rules injected into every brief forever is not a
§10 bug; it is this definition, written here.

No test reaches it: every `UncitedOpenRules` case in `tests/Callboard.Tests/RuleCitationsTests.cs:159-190`
writes repository-scoped rules into `register/`. Neither `change`-scope nor the archive is exercised.

On the question you asked directly — **has §7 left unconditional injection achievable?** Yes,
structurally: hazards and questions are repository-only (`CardScopeRules:19,22`), so archive never
touches them and the "question outlives its change" scenario holds by construction rather than by a
carry-forward, which is exactly what the requirement wanted. The one thing standing between §10 and
that requirement is this predicate, and it is cheaper to fix here than to discover there.

### Blocker 3 — the section's JSON results do not read as one surface.

Eight new result types, and the same three facts are spelled differently in each:

| verb | acting role | timestamp | subject |
|---|---|---|---|
| `*/create` | `ActingRole` | `Timestamp` | `Id` + `FilePath` |
| `*/discharge` | `DischargedBy` | `DischargedAt` | `Id` + `FilePath` |
| `decision supersede` | `DischargedBy` | `DischargedAt` | `SupersedingId`/`SupersededId` |
| `rule compact` | `DischargedBy` | `CompactedAt` | `FamilyId` + `FamilyFilePath` |
| `change archive` | `ArchivedBy` | `ArchivedAt` | `ChangeName` |
| `rule propose-compact` | `ProposedBy` | `ProposedAt` | `Backing` |
| `rule promote` | **absent** | `PromotedAt` | `Id` + `OldFilePath`/`NewFilePath` |

Two of these are wrong rather than merely inconsistent:

1. **`RuleCompactResult.DischargedBy` (`src/Callboard/Cli/RuleCompactResult.cs:28`) is a misnomer.**
   Nothing named in that result is discharged by it — the field carries the acting role, and the
   card that *is* discharged is each absorbed rule. A consumer reading `family_id` and
   `discharged_by` on the same object will read it as the family being discharged.
2. **`RulePromoteResult` (`src/Callboard/Cli/RulePromoteResult.cs:15-27`) reports no acting role at
   all,** and `PromoteRule` writes no attribution to the card either — only `Scope` and `Updated`
   (`src/Callboard/Cards/CardStore.cs:977-980`). Promotion is therefore the one §7 state change the
   record cannot attribute to anyone. Every sibling operation in the section attributes itself:
   discharge writes `discharged_by`, compaction writes `discharged_by` on each member, 7.12 appends
   an attributed comment. This is the degraded-mode promise thinning by one card at a time — the
   file still parses, but "who promoted this rule out of its change?" is answerable only from git.

### Suggested remediation shape (one block, ticks nothing)

1. **Make 7.9's proposal durable**, by the mechanism 7.12 already established: resolve the backing
   set (already done), and record the proposal as an attributed, `to=product-owner` artefact —
   `CardStore.AppendComment` on each backing rule, or a single card, Architect's call. It must
   survive the process, carry the candidate text, the backing ids and the citation counts as
   recorded, and still write nothing to any rule's `status`, `absorbs` or `superseded_by`. Keep the
   existing byte-identity test proving the backing set is unchanged; add one that re-reads the
   record in a fresh call and finds the proposal.
2. **Settle what "live" means for a rule, in one place.** Either archive-aware liveness in
   `RuleCitations` (a change-scoped rule under `callboard/changes/archive/` is not live), or a
   single named predicate both `UncitedOpenRules` and §10 must go through. Tests: a change-scoped
   open rule in an archived change is not queued and does not count toward the ceiling; a
   repository-scoped rule promoted out of that change before archive still is. If the Architect
   prefers the other reading — that an archived change's rules stay live until a human discharges
   them — say so in the thread and pin it with a test, because §10 will otherwise decide it by
   accident.
3. **Normalise the result shapes**: `ActingRole` (or one chosen spelling) on every §7 result
   including `RulePromoteResult`; rename `RuleCompactResult.DischargedBy`; and decide whether
   promotion attributes itself on the card as well as in the response.

### ❓ @architect — a decision, not a defect

**Three conventions now name the subject of a register mutation**, and no block was wrong on its
own:

- `rule|hazard|obligation|decision discharge <path>` — positional **file path**
  (`CommandParser.cs:453`, block A, predates the resolver)
- `decision supersede <id> --supersedes <id>` — positional **id** (`:1809`, block C, "the first §7
  verb built that way from the start")
- `rule promote|compact|promote-constitution --id <id>` — **`--id` flag** (`:1139`, blocks E/F/G)

The Product Owner ruled that identity is the reference and free-text labels stop being an addressing
mechanism; block C read that as reaching the CLI, blocks E/F/G agreed but chose a different spelling,
and block A was never revisited. An agent driving this surface has to remember which of three shapes
each verb takes. Worth settling before §8 adds verbs against it — and note the functional edge:
`discharge <path>` is the only register mutation whose argument stops working when a card moves,
which is the property Option C was rejected for.

### Architectural notes for `## NEXT` (not this block)

1. **The wire-key guard debt — I agree leaving it was right, with a deadline.** `RegisterCardFields`
   has `RegisterCardFieldKeys.All` plus a reflective coverage test after that drift silently
   duplicated frontmatter lines without bound. `CardFrontmatter`, `BlockCardFields`,
   `SectionCardFields` and `FindingCardFields` have hand-listed literals in `CardFileParser.cs:25-53`
   and again in the writer. §7 added no field to any of them, so the debt did not grow here and
   fixing it would have been scope §7 should not take. But the failure mode is *silent record
   corruption*, one of the four ADR-0003 promises, and it is guarded for one of five field types.
   It should land **before** the next section that adds a field to block, section or finding cards —
   not as general cleanup later.
2. **`CeilingPassed` and `UncitedOpenRules` have no production caller.** Sanctioned by the block G
   brief and correctly deferred to §10 — but until §10 lands they are code that ships and never
   runs. Record it as an obligation on §10 rather than leaving it for the next supervisor to
   rediscover as dead scaffolding.
3. **Citation counting is O(rules × cards) full parses** — `UncitedOpenRules` calls `CountCitations`
   per rule and each walks the whole record. Fine for a compaction review; not fine on a per-brief
   path. §10 must not put it behind the working-context response.
4. **Repository-scoped compaction can be proposed but never applied by any verb** — `rule compact`
   requires `--change` and change-scoped members. That is consistent with the spec ("applies
   nothing"), but the loop has no closing move recorded anywhere; §11 should say how a Product

5. **`not-a-register-card` (`CommandDispatcher.cs:1425`) is the `WrongCardKind` shape.** It names a
   kind mismatch and differs from `wrong-card-kind` only in that the expected side is a set of four
