to `product-owner`) does not transfer cleanly, because a proposal has no single subject card: it has
candidate text that exists nowhere yet and a backing set of N rules. Writing the same proposal onto
all N is duplication, and duplication of a thing the Product Owner must later act on once.

else does. If that means adding creation surface for a kind block A did not cover, **stop and post

**Why `question` is correct and not a stretch.** Register defines the shape itself — repository-scoped,
"continues to surface to the role that owes its answer", outliving the change that raised it. A
repository-scoped compaction proposal is precisely a question owed by the Product Owner: *should
these rules become this family?* `obligation` names a section expected to discharge it and `decision`
is capability-scoped; both would need a required field bent away from its documented meaning, which
is how a record starts lying.

section close over open undeferred questions), 9.9 (refuse marking a question answered without a
decision reference or inline answer) and 9.10 (refuse advancing a card blocked by an open Product
Owner question). **Every one is a refusal about a question's lifecycle; none is creation.** A
creation verb gives §9 something to refuse against — it does not decide how answering or deferring
works. Block A set this exact precedent: it created five kinds and left their lifecycle rules to the
sections that own them.

### My three findings — closed

**Blocker 1 — closed, and both properties hold at once.** `RunRuleProposeCompact`
(`src/Callboard/Cli/CommandDispatcher.cs:1933-2032`) now creates one `question` card at the
caller-named `--proposal-file`, owner `product-owner`, body carrying candidate text, proposer,
and each backing rule with its citation count (`BuildProposalCardBody:2043-2059`). **Durable**: it
goes through `CardStore.CreateCard` — the same locked, create-only atomic path every other creation
verb uses, no sixth way to put a card on disk — and the body is plain Markdown, so the Product Owner
reading the file sees exactly what a JSON caller sees. **Inert**: I read the whole function looking
for the failure mode you named, and the write is structurally incapable of touching the backing set
— the only path passed to `CreateCard` is `parsed.ProposalFilePath`, `resolved.FilePath` is never
handed to a write of any kind, and creation happens *after* the resolve/validate/count loop
completes, so a refusal on any backing rule returns before a card exists. Adding a write path did
not cost the inertness.

**Blocker 2 — closed, and the split is the right one.** `ResolveLiveRecordDirectories`
(`src/Callboard/Cards/CardLayout.cs:141-168`) and `ResolveRecordDirectories` are now two different
questions, and only `UncitedOpenRules` was narrowed. `CountCitations` staying archive-inclusive is
correct and I want that on the record as a deliberate call, not an inconsistency: a citation is
evidence someone leaned on a rule, and that does not stop being true when the citing card's change
archives. The two new `RuleCitationsTests` cases pin both directions, including the one I was most
worried about (a rule promoted out *before* its change archived stays queued) — archive does not
sweep away something already live.

**Blocker 3 — closed, and it went further than I asked.** `ActingRole` is now the single spelling
across every §7 result *and* matches §5/§6's existing use, so the surface got more coherent than it
was before §7 opened. `PromoteRule` (`src/Callboard/Cards/CardStore.cs:980-1003`) records the
promotion as one attributed comment inside the write that already moves the card — one
`AtomicWrite`, no second lock, and `CardCommentImmutabilityTests`' inventory entry updated rather
than left stale, which is the file whose whole job is catching that.

### Blocker — `question create` cannot name the role that owes the answer, and a test now pins that it does not

Card-model, "Ownership names whose turn it is":

> Every card SHALL carry an `owner` naming **the single role whose turn it is to act** […]
> Ownership SHALL be queryable, so that any role can ask what it owns.

Register, on the question that outlives its change:

> **THEN** the question remains open and **continues to surface to the role that owes its answer**.

For a `question`, `owner` is not one attribute among several — it is the entire routing mechanism,
and this section shipped no way to change it (`CardStore.TransferOwnership` exists in the domain and
is reachable from no CLI verb; I checked every call site).

`question create` (`src/Callboard/Cli/CommandParser.cs:1838-1843` → `CommandDispatcher.cs:1408-1425`)
goes through the shared `ParseCardCreate`/`CreateCard` pair, which sets `owner` to `--role` — the
**acting** role. So `question create … --role worker` produces a card owned by `worker`:
the raiser, who is precisely the role waiting rather than the role whose turn it is.
`CommandDispatcherQuestionCreateTests.cs:41` asserts `CardOwner.Worker` and so pins it.

The two creation paths for this one kind now disagree about what `owner` means:

| path | owner | reading |
|---|---|---|
| `RunRuleProposeCompact` (`:2010`) | `CardOwner.ProductOwner` | the role that owes the answer |
| `question create` (`:1421`) | `parsed.ActingRole` | the role that raised it |

The proposal path is right, and it is right only because it bypasses the verb and calls `CreateCard`
directly. Every question raised through the verb routes to its raiser, permanently, with no shipped
command able to move it — which is the register scenario read backwards.

Note where this came from, because it is not carelessness: your own authorising ruling named the
correct semantic ("a repository compaction proposal is precisely a question **owed by** the Product
Owner"), the worker's `❓` proposed `owner = product-owner`, and then "minimal, the same shape as
block A's five verbs" routed it through a helper built for four kinds where owner-as-raiser is
harmless because nothing routes on it. Each step was reasonable; the sum is a routing field set to
the wrong role. That is the shape this review exists for, and it landed after my last pass, so this
is its first look.

**Remediation shape.** `question create` takes the answerer explicitly — `--owed-by <role>`
(required; no default, since guessing is how the wrong one gets written), passed to `CreateCard` as
the owner while `--role` keeps meaning the acting role, as it does everywhere else. Update
`CommandDispatcherQuestionCreateTests.cs:41` to assert the owed role, not the caller's, and add the
case where the two differ. No lifecycle, no transfer verb, no `--owner` on any other kind: this
stays inside the creation-only boundary. `RunRuleProposeCompact` needs no change — it already
expresses the right thing and should keep calling `CreateCard` directly.

### The two questions you asked me

**1. Is `question create`'s boundary where it should be? Yes — the *lifecycle* boundary is right.**
Creation here, answer/defer/blocked-by in §9, is the same split block A used for five kinds and it
gives 9.7/9.9/9.10 something to refuse against instead of forcing them to invent creation as a side
effect. What sits on the wrong side of that boundary is not a lifecycle verb — it is *who owns a
brand-new question*, which is a creation-time fact and therefore §7's, not §9's. Fix that and the
boundary is exactly where I would have drawn it. I would also rather §9 inherited a verb than a
convention, so I think authorising it was the right call.

**2. Is the subject-naming deferral defensible? Yes — plainly, and it does not block.** You have it
right on all three counts: §7's `--id` is the correct convention, harmonising means rewriting
§1–§6's shipped surface, and that is the Product Owner's call rather than something to fold into a
remediation carrying one round to converge. Binding `--id` from §8 stops the drift growing while the
decision is pending, which is the part that mattered to me — my concern was a surface that keeps
accreting conventions, not the two that already exist. Raised as its own decision is the right home
for it, and I would not hold the section for it.

counting's cost on a per-brief path, repository compaction's missing closing move) all still stand
unchanged — the last one now has a card to hang on, which is an improvement.

### The fourth blocker — closed, and it closed the requirement with it

`question create` now takes a required `--owed-by <role>`, parsed in its own function rather than
through `ParseCardCreate` (`src/Callboard/Cli/CommandParser.cs:1839-1916`), and `RunQuestionCreate`
passes it as the card's owner while `--role` keeps meaning the acting role
(`src/Callboard/Cli/CommandDispatcher.cs:1427-1445`). The refusal text says why it is not defaulted
("the raiser and the answerer are usually different roles"), which is the right thing to put in a
message a caller will hit.

The part worth naming: **this is what actually made register's second archive scenario true.** In my
first review I recorded "Question outlives its change" as holding by construction, because questions
are repository-scoped and archive never touches them. That was only half of it — the scenario says
the question *continues to surface to the role that owes its answer*, and until this round the only
creation verb could not name that role. The section now satisfies that scenario through its own
surface rather than by accident of scope.

Taking the verb apart rather than the report: `ParseQuestionCreate` refuses a missing `--owed-by`
and an unparseable one before any write; `CreateCard` receives `parsed.OwedByRole` as owner and
`MapCardCreateOutcome` receives `parsed.ActingRole` separately, so the two facts are carried
distinctly all the way through rather than reconstructed at the end. The test that pinned the defect
was changed with the code and now asserts both directions (`CardOwner.ProductOwner`, and explicitly
`NotEqual(CardOwner.Worker)`), which is the assertion that would have caught the original.

### The hole the fix opened — genuinely closed, and I checked the shape rather than the instance

The reviewer is right that making `actingRole` a parameter turned a self-check into caller-trust for
all six creation verbs, and right that the mutation proved it. `CreationVerb_ResponseActingRole_
MatchesOwnerReadBackFromDisk` closes it properly: the comparison is against `Frontmatter.Owner` read
back through a *fresh* `CardStore.ReadCard`, not off the response object, so the two reads are
genuinely independent; all five sharing verbs are covered; and rooting every case on `--role worker`
is load-bearing rather than incidental — the reviewer demonstrated that the same mutation passes
under `architect` because the hardcode and the caller's value coincide. `MemberData` over reflection
is the correct call here and the reasoning given for it is sound: there is no single type whose
members are "the five verbs", so there is no shape to reflect over.

**Does anything else of that shape remain? No removed self-check — but one weakness, and it is
section-wide rather than local.** I classified every `ActingRole` assignment in the dispatcher: six
read back from the written card or the outcome, seven echo the parsed value. Only
`MapCardCreateOutcome` ever *lost* a read-back; the other echoes were echoes from birth and claim
nothing they don't have. What does generalise is the blind spot the reviewer found, not the defect:
`CommandDispatcherRulePromoteTests:39,48` asserts both the response's `actingRole` and the promotion

either would survive that test exactly as it survived in `RunRuleCreate`. Nothing is wrong today;
the test simply cannot discriminate. That belongs in `## NEXT` as a habit, not in a fix block.

### The register spec, requirement by requirement

| requirement | state |
|---|---|
| Rules and hazards injected unconditionally | **Ground prepared, §10 delivers.** Hazards are repository-only, so archive cannot reach them; "live rules" now has one correct statement (`ResolveLiveRecordDirectories`). §7 precludes nothing. |
| Register kinds have a two-state lifecycle | **Met.** `open`/`discharged` for all four kinds, flow states refused (`invalid-register-status`), `owed_by` required on obligations and resolved to a real section, decisions carry both supersession links. |
| The register lives above the change | **Met, both scenarios.** Archive settles change-scoped obligations and moves one directory; register and decisions are never enumerated. No carry-forward step exists. The question scenario now holds through the surface, per above. |
| Promotion is retrospective and preserves the link | **Met.** `rule promote --id` moves the file keeping id, body and thread, and now records who did it in the same write; `rule author --earned-from` creates a new card recording its findings, which are unchanged. No durability flag anywhere. |
| Rules compact into families by supersession | **Met.** Absorbed rules are discharged and carry `superseded_by`; the family carries `absorbs`; every member stays retrievable by identity. The architect constraint lives in `CompactRules` itself, so both entry points inherit it. `rule propose-compact` records a durable `question` and applies nothing. |
| Register size triggers review, never eviction | **Met as domain logic; not yet observable.** Counting, the soft ceiling and the uncited queue are correct and prohibition-respecting, and nothing retires anything — but no CLI verb reaches them, so under ADR-0001 no caller can see this requirement work until §10 wires it. Sanctioned and correct for §7; carried into `## NEXT` as an explicit obligation rather than an assumption. |
| Hazards carry a verification condition | **Met.** Both fields refused by their own spec-named codes at raise time; discharge covers the lapse. "Ceases to be injected" is §10's, and reachable. |
| The project constitution stays outside agent control | **Met.** Refuses every role including `product-owner`, never names the file, and leaves a durable attributed comment addressed to the Product Owner. |

### The section-level lenses, one last pass

**Refusal coverage as a set.** 236 sites, 53 codes, re-derived rather than counted forward. The two
granularity rulings hold everywhere I checked: spec-named facts have their own codes
(`hazard-missing-condition`/`-cadence`, `obligation-missing-owed-by`, `empty-absorb-set`), incidental
absent flags share `missing-argument`, and role authorisation is one `role-not-permitted` covering
both `CompactRules` and 7.12. Every transition §7 made reachable passes a guard: creation through
`CardScopeRules` plus per-kind required fields, discharge through kind/status checks, promotion
through scope checks, compaction through role, scope, status and self/duplicate-member checks before
any lock, supersession through the same shape plus an acyclicity argument that holds at any chain
length, archive through name validation, existence, already-archived and an unreadable-file
fail-closed. I could not find a transition with no guard in front of it.

**CLI surface coherence.** One verb naming its subject three ways is still the section's roughest
edge, correctly deferred to the Product Owner with `--id` binding from §8 — I said in round two that
does not block and it still does not. Nothing this round widened it: `--owed-by` and `--proposal-file`
are new flags on their own verbs, not new ways to name an existing verb's subject.

**Record/index divergence.** None. §7 added no index column and no read path that treats the index as
authoritative; `IndexPopulator` was refactored onto the shared directory resolver so population and
resolution cannot drift, and it deliberately kept the archive-inclusive walk.

**Identity addressing.** Even. Every card-to-card reference — `--section`, `--owed-by` (obligation),
`--supersedes`, `--absorbs`, `--earned-from`, `--id` — resolves through `ResolveCardReference`, and
the one free-text match left (`RuleCitations.NamesRuleId`) is an advisory count that gates nothing,
with the structured alternative rejected by the Product Owner on the record.

**Duplicated abstractions and dead scaffolding.** The multi-card write paths are one discipline, not
four lookalikes: `RecordFinding`, `SupersedeDecision` and `CompactRules` share the read-fresh-under-
lock/write/rollback shape with deterministic lock ordering and each states its own failure guarantee
honestly, and `PromoteRule` folded its new attribution into the write it already had rather than
growing a second phase. `rule propose-compact` writes through the same `CardStore.CreateCard`
primitive as `question create` rather than inventing a second way onto disk. No superseded scaffolding
survives; the two unwired functions are deferred surface, named below rather than left silent.

The binding ADRs hold across the sum, not just per block: one CLI surface with no daemon and no
interactive path, every write under `WithLock` through `AtomicWrite` or a same-filesystem rename,
the index derived and never a lock, refusals failing closed, comments append-only, identities never
recycled, and `callboard/` legible without the tool — including a compacted family, where the
back-link on each absorbed rule means an over-abstract family can be unpicked by reading files.

### For `## NEXT` — what §8 onward inherits

1. **The writer/parser wire-key guard, with a deadline.** `RegisterCardFields` has
   `RegisterCardFieldKeys.All` plus a reflective coverage test, after that drift silently duplicated
   frontmatter lines without bound. `CardFrontmatter`, `BlockCardFields`, `SectionCardFields` and
   `FindingCardFields` still hand-list their keys twice (`CardFileParser.cs:25-53` and again in the
   writer). §7 added no field to any of them, so the debt did not grow — **it should be closed before
   the next section that adds a field to block, section or finding cards**, because the failure mode
   is silent record corruption and it is currently guarded for one of five field types.
2. **§10 owes the register its surface.** `RuleCitations.CeilingPassed` and `UncitedOpenRules` have
   no production caller (verified: declaration and doc references only). Until §10 wires them, "size
   triggers review" is correct code no caller can reach. §10 must also use
   `ResolveLiveRecordDirectories` — not `ResolveRecordDirectories` — for anything it calls "live".
3. **Do not put `CountCitations` on a per-brief path.** `UncitedOpenRules` calls it per rule and each
   call walks and parses the whole record; it is O(rules × cards). Fine for a compaction review, not
   for the working-context response.
4. **Root attribution assertions on a non-default role.** The `architect`-shaped stand-in that hid
   the `MapCardCreateOutcome` mutation is a property of how the tests are written, not of that one
   verb; `CommandDispatcherRulePromoteTests:39,48` has the same weakness today.
5. **`--owed-by` now takes two different argument types** — a section card id on `obligation create`,
   a role on `question create`. Defensible (the concept is the same; the answerer differs by kind),
   but §9 adds question verbs against this flag, so decide deliberately rather than inheriting it.
6. **`question create`'s response does not report the card's owner** — a caller gets `actingRole`
   (the raiser) and a `null` `owedBy` (that field is the obligation register field, not this one).
   The record is right; the response is just less informative than the card. Worth closing when §9
   grows the question result shape.
7. **Repository-scoped compaction still has no closing move.** A proposal is now a durable question
   owned by the Product Owner, which is a real improvement — but no verb applies a decided family.
   §11 should say how the Product Owner's answer reaches the record.

Three rounds, four blockers, all four closed on the code rather than in the report. §7 is done.

contradictory one:

- `review-certification`: the three `building` mentions → `briefed`
- `work-lifecycle`: the diagram gains `fix-before-land` (in-review → briefed) and
  `recertification-refused` (approved → briefed), both `round += 1`
- `tasks.md`: 8.5 and 8.9 reworded to match

**Architect call inside that ruling:** `fix-before-land` is a **distinct named edge**, not a reuse of
`changes-requested`, despite sharing From/To. The transition name is persisted in the card's history
(`CardBlockTransitionEntry`), and recording a dispositioned nit as `changes-requested` would
misreport what happened. `BlockFlowTransitions.AvailableFrom` returns a list and lookup is by name,
so two edges sharing From/To is already supported — `in-review` simply gains a third available
transition.

**[architect]** **A standing fact for every block in this section: the tool does not shell out.**
Verified at section open — `System.Diagnostics.Process` appears nowhere in `src/Callboard` source
(only in build artefacts under `obj/`/`bin/`). §5 established the discipline with gates: the tool
never *runs* a gate, it records the exit code its caller supplies, and `GateResult`'s own doc comment
is explicit that the exit code is the only accepted evidence. §8 inherits this without exception:

- **8.11 "gates re-run green"** reads recorded `GateResult`s at the card's *current* round via
  `BlockCardFields.GateStatusOf` — it does not run `make gates`.
- **8.11 "difference confined to the sites of the dispositioned nits"** compares **caller-supplied**
  changed paths against the sites recorded on the nits. The tool does not run `git diff`.
- **8.2 `reviewed_state`** is a caller-supplied string naming the state, explicitly including
  uncommitted working-tree content. The tool does not resolve or verify a SHA.

A block that finds itself wanting to invoke `git` or a gate has misread the requirement — stop and
report rather than adding the first subprocess call to this codebase.

**[architect]** §8 carved into four blocks. 8.13 (role-bounding) is deliberately **not** in block A
even though block A implements approve's half of it: the task covers *approval and recertification*,
so it ticks in block C when both verbs enforce it. Block A still ships the refusal — a refusal that
fails open is this project's named hazard, not something to defer to a later block.

| block | tasks | deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| A | 8.1, 8.2, 8.3 | `approve` as a binary verdict: `reviewed_state`, enumerated claims and limits, the two approval refusals |
| B | 8.4, 8.5, 8.6, 8.7 | nits as dispositioned addressed comments; the `fix-before-land` edge; `defer`→obligation, `decline`→decision |
| C | 8.8, 8.9, 8.10, 8.13 | `recertify` with per-claim assert/refuse; the `recertification-refused` edge; the one-per-approval bound; role-bounding both verbs |
| D | 8.11, 8.12 | the mechanical preconditions as refuse-only, and the test that green confers no claim |

**[architect]** **Block A brief — 8.1, 8.2, 8.3.** `approve` as a binary certification of one exact
state, enumerating what it claims and what it does not.

**Tasks**

- 8.1 Implement the binary verdict, refusing any approval carrying unresolved blocking findings
- 8.2 Record `reviewed_state` as the exact state certified, including uncommitted content
- 8.3 Refuse an approval that enumerates no claims and no limits

**Binding spec — `review-certification`, two requirements**

> A review verdict SHALL be exactly one of `approve` or `request-changes`. The system SHALL NOT offer
> a verdict combining approval with outstanding findings.
>
> An `approve` SHALL certify one exact state, recorded as the card's `reviewed_state`. An approval
> SHALL name that state explicitly, including any uncommitted working-tree content it covers.

> An approval SHALL enumerate the claims it makes and state what it does not establish. Certification
> text SHALL be written to be actionable by a reviewer who did not author it, because recertification
> may be performed by a different reviewer reading it cold.

Scenarios: approval records the state it certifies; approve-with-nits is unavailable (refuse, and
direct the reviewer to `approve` with dispositioned nits or to `request-changes`); approval without
enumerated claims is refused (refuse, and state that certification text is read by a later reviewer
who did not write it).

**Architect readings and calls — implement these, do not re-litigate them; challenge in-thread if you
think one is wrong**

1. **`block approve` is its own verb, and it is the only door to `approved`.** §5 already has the
   `approve` edge reachable via `block transition <path> approve`. That path must now **refuse**,
   naming `block approve`, because a transition through it would move a block to `approved` carrying
   no certification at all — an uncertified approval is exactly what this section exists to prevent.
   One door, and the certification is stamped in the same write as the transition.
2. **8.1 is about the verdict *surface*, not a scan of finding cards.** `findings` (§6) never defined
   an open/resolved lifecycle — finding cards carry `live`/`degraded`/`unreadable` staleness, nothing
   else — so "unresolved blocking findings" has no referent to scan for, and inventing one here would
   be §6's capability, not §8's. `proposal.md`'s OQ-7 row settles the intent: *"'approve with nits' as
   a verdict variant — Deleted; approve is binary."* So: the verb offers **no** way to attach findings
   to an approval, and an invocation that attempts to combine the two is refused with the spec's own
   redirect. **Reviewer: this reading is the thing to challenge if you disagree — say so in-thread.**
3. **`--state` is caller-supplied text, verified against nothing.** Per the section-open post: the
   tool does not shell out. It does not resolve a SHA, does not ask git what is uncommitted, does not
   validate the string's shape. A reviewer certifying uncommitted work writes something like
   `afaad73 + uncommitted working tree (src/Callboard/Cards/CardStore.cs)` and that whole string is
   what `reviewed_state` records. Refuse an empty/whitespace-only `--state`; that is all.
4. **Claims and limits need stable identity from day one.** 8.8 re-asserts an existing approval's
   claims *individually*, so each claim must be addressable later. Do not store them as a
   comma-joined frontmatter list — claim text is prose and will contain commas. Use the append-only
   HTML-comment sequence the format already establishes for `callboard:handover`,
   `callboard:transition` and `callboard:verdict` (see `CardFileFormat`), with each claim carrying
   its own id. Limits are part of the same certification record; they are never individually
   asserted, so they need no ids.
5. **8.3 refuses on "no claims **and** no limits" — that is the spec's own conjunction.** An approval
   with claims but no limits is permitted, as is one with limits but no claims. Do not tighten this to
   require both.
6. **`--id` binds** (§7's settled ruling): name the block by `--id`, not by positional path. Do not
   touch the argument shape of any §1–§6 verb in passing — harmonising those is an open Product Owner
   decision.

**Standing constraints for this section**

- **No subprocess, anywhere.** `System.Diagnostics.Process` appears nowhere in `src/Callboard` source
  and this block does not introduce it.
- **Wire-key drift guard (carried from §7's close, item A).** `RegisterCardFields` has a single shared
  key declaration (`RegisterCardFieldKeys`) that writer and parser both read; `BlockCardFields` does
  **not**, and when that drifted in §7 every parse→write cycle silently duplicated a frontmatter line
  and compounded, green over 544 tests. §7's parting note says it closes *before the next section that
  adds a field to any of them*. **That is this block if you add a field to `BlockCardFields` — close
  it first, in that case.** `ReviewedState` already exists there, so 8.2 may well need no new field;
  if the certification record lives entirely in the body sequence, the guard obligation does not fire
  — but whatever new keys the certification sequence introduces get a single shared declaration from
  the start, not two hand-maintained lists.
- **Refusal-code granularity** (settled three times in §7): a refusal the spec *names* gets its own
  code; an incidental missing flag gets `missing-argument`/`missing-flag-value`. Where several
  refusals name one fact differing only in a parameter, collapse them into one code whose *message*
  carries the parameter. **Re-derive the refusal set mechanically; never increment a remembered
  number** — that has been wrong by arithmetic twice.
- **Validate everything before writing anything**, one global lock order, and state the failure
  guarantee honestly rather than claiming atomicity you do not have. Five existing multi-phase writers
  already do this — extend the discipline, do not invent a sixth shape.
- **Attribution assertions root on a non-default role** (§7 item E): assert with a role the code would
  *not* default to, so a hardcode cannot survive the test.

verbatim; do not summarise them. A test per refusal rule, per the amended S5.

**[architect]** **Block B brief — 8.4, 8.5, 8.6, 8.7.** Nits as dispositioned addressed comments: the
mechanism that stops a nit lapsing by neglect.

**Tasks**

- 8.4 Implement nits as addressed comments carrying a disposition

**Binding spec — `review-certification`, "Nits carry a disposition"**

> A nit SHALL be raised as an addressed comment, not as a card, so that raising one is no more costly
> than commenting. Every nit SHALL receive a disposition chosen by the architect, of
> `fix-before-land`, `defer` or `decline`. A reviewer MAY mark a nit as required; that marking SHALL
> NOT bind the architect's disposition.

| Disposition | Outcome |
|---|---|
| `fix-before-land` | Stays inline; the block returns to `briefed`, `round` increments, and the amended state requires re-certification |
| `defer` | Promoted to an `obligation` card naming what discharges it |
| `decline` | Promoted to a `decision` card recording the reason the code is right as it stands |

> A nit SHALL cease to be live only through one of these three dispositions. It SHALL NOT lapse by
> neglect.

Note the `briefed` in that table is the **Product Owner's ruling of this session** (`afaad73`), not the
text §8 was written with. `work-lifecycle`'s diagram now carries the two new edges — read the current
spec, not a memory of it.

**Architect readings and calls — binding; challenge in-thread if you think one is wrong**

1. **A disposition is a *later* comment, never a mutation of the nit.** Comments are append-only and
   `CardComment` offers no mutation path by construction. §4 already settled the idiom for exactly
   this shape: resolution is recorded by a subsequent comment naming the one it resolves
   (`CardComment.Resolves`), *because* a settable "am I resolved" bit on the comment would be the
   forbidden after-the-fact edit. A disposition is the same species — a later comment naming the nit
   it dispositions and carrying the chosen value. **Do not add a mutable field to `CardComment`.**
2. **A nit records its sites, and block D depends on you for them.** 8.11 gates recertification on
   "the difference between certified and amended states is confined to the sites of the dispositioned
   nits". If a nit does not record where it applies, block D cannot be built without retrofitting the
   wire format — the one thing §7 taught us is expensive. Record sites now (repeatable `--site`),
   even though nothing in this block reads them back.
3. **`required` is recorded and never consulted when validating a disposition.** The spec is explicit
   that it "SHALL NOT bind the architect's disposition". **Ship a test that declines a `required`
   nit and succeeds** — the marking is advisory, and a test is the only thing that keeps it advisory
   once someone later "helpfully" adds a check.
4. **HAZARD — `round` must increment once per round, not once per fix-before-land nit.** Three nits
   dispositioned `fix-before-land` in one sitting are one return to `briefed`, not three, and
   certainly not `round += 3`. Once the block has left `in-review`, the edge is no longer available
   from its current state — do not "helpfully" re-apply it. Record the disposition regardless (the
   nit is still dispositioned; that is 8.7's business), and make the transition the part that happens
   at most once. **This needs its own test with at least two fix-before-land nits asserting a single
   increment.** I rate this the most likely defect in the block.
5. **8.7 binds *every* exit from `in-review`, including block A's `block approve`.** The requirement is
   "a block is moved out of `in-review` while a nit raised against it has no disposition". That is
   `approve`, `changes-requested`, and `fix-before-land` itself — a fix-before-land disposition on nit
   1 must still refuse if nit 2 is undispositioned. You will be modifying block A's `block approve`
   path to enforce this; that is expected, not scope creep. The refusal **names the undispositioned
   nits**, per the scenario.
6. **Dispositioning is architect-only.** The spec says the disposition is "chosen by the architect".
   I read that as role-bounding the verb. This is the reading in this block most open to challenge —
   it is stated as an attribution, not as a refusal requirement, and §9 owns the role-refusal family.
   Say so in-thread if you read it differently.
7. **Verb surface** — `--id` binds (§7):
   - `nit raise --id <block-id> --role <role> [--required] --site <path> [--site <path>…]`, body on
     redirected stdin per ADR-0001/D1 and `StdinBodyReader`. Addressed to the architect.
   - `nit disposition --id <nit-id> --role architect --disposition fix-before-land|defer|decline`,
     body on stdin (the reason — load-bearing for `decline`, which becomes a decision card whose whole
     content is the reason the code is right as it stands).

**Standing constraints**

- **`defer` and `decline` are multi-card writes.** Each creates a card *and* appends the disposition
  comment. Validate everything before writing anything, take locks in one global order, and **state
  the failure guarantee honestly rather than claiming atomicity you do not have**. Five writers
  already do this — `RecordFinding`, `SupersedeDecision`, `CompactRules`, `PromoteRule`,
  `ArchiveChange`. Extend the discipline; §7's parting note is explicit: **do not add a sixth shape.**
- **`BlockFlowTransitions` is a closed, compile-checked table** and this is the first block to add an
  edge to it. `in-review` gains a third available transition, so every refusal message that enumerates
  available transitions changes shape — check the existing tests that assert those strings.
- **No subprocess.** Still true, still absolute.
- **Refusal-code granularity**: a refusal the spec names gets its own code; an incidental missing flag
  gets `missing-argument`/`missing-flag-value`; several refusals naming one fact differing only by a
  parameter collapse into one code whose message carries the parameter. **Re-derive the set
  mechanically — never increment a remembered number.**
- **Attribution assertions root on a non-default role** (§7 item E). This block is full of
  `architect`-authored writes, which is precisely the value the code would default to — assert with a
  role that would not survive a hardcode.
- **`--owed-by` means two different things across two verbs** (§7 item F): a section card id on
  `obligation create`, a role on `question create`. `defer` creates an obligation — do not conflate
  them.

**[architect]** **Block B — one blocker, found before handing to the reviewer. Order-dependent
correctness in `DispositionNit`'s fix-before-land arm.**

`CardStore.cs:760` gates the transition on **this call's** disposition being `FixBeforeLand`, then
checks that no nit is left undispositioned. Both conditions are individually right; requiring them on
the *same call* is not. Walk two nits:

1. nit1 dispositioned `fix-before-land` → nit2 still live → edge correctly withheld.
2. nit2 dispositioned `defer` → `LiveUndispositionedNitIds` is now empty, but
   `ReferenceEquals(disposition, NitDisposition.FixBeforeLand)` is **false for this call** → the edge
   is never applied by anyone.

The block strands in `in-review`. `round` never increments, it never returns to `briefed`, and the
amended state never requires re-certification — the spec's three stated consequences of
`fix-before-land`, none of which happen.

**And the second face, which is worse than stranding.** With every nit now dispositioned,
`LiveUndispositionedNitIds` is empty, so 8.7 no longer refuses — `block approve` is *permitted*. A
block carrying a `fix-before-land` nit whose fix was never made can be approved and certified. That is
the exact inversion of the requirement: `fix-before-land` exists to guarantee the fix lands before the
certification does.

It works only when the fix-before-land disposition happens to be **last**. Correctness that depends on
the order the architect dispositions nits in is not correctness.
`NitDisposition_TwoFixBeforeLandNitsInOneRound_IncrementsRoundExactlyOnce` passes because two
fix-before-land nits put a fix-before-land call last by construction; there is no test for the mixed
ordering, which is why this is green.

**The fix is the reframing, not a patch.** The question is not "is *this* disposition fix-before-land"
but **"does this card, now that nothing is undispositioned, carry any fix-before-land nit this
round?"** — a property of the card's whole thread, not of the call. That is the same lesson
`CardCommentRouting`'s own doc comment already records for resolution: compute it over the thread
rather than storing it on one entry. `LiveUndispositionedNitIds` is already the thread-level query;
this wants its sibling.

Item 4 of the brief was right that `round` must increment at most once. It was **my framing that was
too narrow** — I described the hazard as repeated increments and you defended against exactly that,
so the omission is as much mine as yours. The invariant is two-sided: **at most once, and at least
once when any fix-before-land nit was dispositioned this round.** You only had the first half.

**Required tests** — the mixed orderings, both ways round:

- fix-before-land then defer → block ends in `briefed`, `round` incremented exactly once
- defer then fix-before-land → same end state (this already passes; pin it so the two cannot diverge)
- fix-before-land then decline → same
- after the above, `block approve` is refused (or unavailable) until the block has been through
  `briefed` — the second face above, asserted directly rather than implied

**[architect]** **Block C brief — 8.8, 8.9, 8.10, 8.13.** `recertify`: re-asserting an existing claim
set over an amended state, claim by claim, without a full re-audit.

**Tasks**

- 8.8 Implement `recertify` with individually assertable and refusable claims
- 8.9 Implement per-claim refusal returning the block to `briefed` without re-stamping `reviewed_state`
- 8.10 Enforce at most one recertification per approval
- 8.13 Restrict approval and recertification to `reviewer` and `supervisor`

**Binding spec — `review-certification`, "Recertification re-asserts an existing claim set" and
"Recertification is bounded"** (read both in full; the second is split between this block and block D).

> Each claim SHALL be individually assertable or refusable. The reviewer SHALL re-derive each claim
> against the code; reading the difference between the certified and amended states SHALL NOT be
> sufficient, because a difference confined to the expected sites has been observed to be green over a
> real defect.
>
> A successful recertification SHALL re-stamp `reviewed_state` to the amended state. A refusal of any
> claim SHALL be a first-class outcome that returns the block to `briefed` and increments `round`.

> The system SHALL permit at most one recertification per approval. A further amendment after a
> recertification SHALL require a new round.

Scenarios: per-claim refusal returns the block (three claims, second refused → **all three outcomes
recorded**, `reviewed_state` **not** re-stamped, block to `briefed`, `round` incremented); all claims
re-asserted → re-stamp without incrementing `round`; second recertification refused.

**Architect readings and calls — binding; challenge in-thread if you think one is wrong**

1. **Claims already have stable identity — use it.** Block A's `callboard:claim` lines each carry an
   id precisely so this block can address them individually. Do not invent a second addressing scheme,
   and do not address a claim by its text or its ordinal position.
2. **Every claim must receive an outcome; a recertification that silently omits one is refused.** The
   spec's scenario records *all three* outcomes for three claims. A recertification naming two of
   three leaves the third in exactly the undefined limbo the nit-disposition rule exists to prevent —
   same disease, same cure. Refuse, naming the claims with no outcome.
3. **The `recertification-refused` edge is `approved → briefed`**, `round += 1`, per the Product
   Owner's ruling at `afaad73`. `BlockFlowTransitions` is a closed compile-checked table; `approved`
   currently has exactly one edge (`land`) and gains a second. Reachable only through `recertify`,
   refused from `block transition` the same way `approve` and `fix-before-land` already are.
4. **On refusal, `reviewed_state` is left exactly as it was.** Not cleared, not blanked, not updated —
   the previously certified state remains the last thing genuinely certified, and that is true. Assert
   it byte-identical after a refused recertification.
5. **A successful recertification does not increment `round`.** The spec is explicit. It re-stamps
   `reviewed_state` and nothing else moves.
6. **8.10's bound attaches to the approval, not to the card.** "At most one recertification **per
   approval**" — a block approved, recertified, sent back to `briefed`, rebuilt, and approved again is
   on a *new* approval and gets a fresh recertification. Do not implement this as a boolean on the
   card that never resets. The natural reading: count recertifications recorded since the current
   approval.
7. **The tool cannot enforce "the reviewer SHALL re-derive each claim".** That sentence governs a
   human, and no flag can distinguish a re-derived assertion from a rubber-stamped one. **Do not
   pretend otherwise** — do not add a `--re-derived` flag or any affordance implying the tool checked.
   Surface the obligation in the response text where the reviewer will read it, and state plainly in
   the doc comment that this is unenforceable by construction. This project's whole thesis is refusing
   what it can and being honest about what it cannot; a flag that records a promise is the failure
   mode, not the feature.
8. **8.13 ticks here.** Block A already role-bound `block approve` to `reviewer`/`supervisor`; do the
   same for `recertify` and tick the task once both hold. `CardStore.IsApprovingRole` already exists —
   reuse it rather than writing a second predicate.
9. **Out of scope: the mechanical preconditions.** Gates re-run green, and the difference confined to
   nit sites, are **8.11 and block D**. Do not implement them here and do not stub them. Block C's
   `recertify` is permitted to proceed without them; block D adds refusals in front of it.

**Standing constraints**

- **No subprocess.** Still absolute. `--state` is caller-supplied text, verified against nothing.
- **The two defects this section has already produced were both "green tests over a real defect"**, and

- **Attribution assertions root on a non-default role** (§7 item E).

**1. Is there a path out of `approved` once the one recertification is spent? No — and that is a
blocker.**

Trace: `BlockFlowTransitions.AvailableFrom(BlockFlowState.Approved)` returns exactly `[Land,
RecertificationRefused]` (`BlockFlowTransitions.cs:241`). `RecertificationRefused` is reachable only
through `CardStore.RecordRecertification` when at least one claim is refused
(`CardStore.cs:539–551`); `block transition <id> recertification-refused` is refused outright at
parse (`CommandParser.cs:189–199`, `recertification-refused-via-transition-refused`), proven by
`BlockTransition_RecertificationRefused_Refuses_AndLeavesTheCardByteIdentical`. A *successful*
recertification (`CardStore.cs:526–537`) leaves `Frontmatter.Status` untouched — the card stays
`approved`, `Round` untouched — and appends a comment with `IsRecertification: true`.

Now call `block recertify` again on that same card, for any reason, including a genuine further
amendment: `approvedAt` (`CardStore.cs:600–607`) is still the timestamp of the original `approve`
transition — nothing in the successful path touches `Transitions` — so `commentsSinceApproval`
still includes the recertification comment just appended, and `CardCommentRouting.HasRecertification`
returns `true` (`CardStore.cs:609–612`). The call is refused `recertification-already-performed`,
and the refusal message itself says: *"a further amendment requires a new round"*
(`CommandDispatcher.cs:1317–1320`). But nothing in this diff, or in the codebase as it stands, gives
the caller a way to *get* a new round from `approved` short of `land`. The only two doors out of
`approved` are `land` (terminal — moves to `landed`) and the now-permanently-refused
`recertification-refused`.

Concretely: reviewer approves a block, certifies it, successfully recertifies once (all claims held,
`reviewed_state` re-stamped). More amendments land in the working tree before anyone lands the
block. The reviewer now has no legal way to send the block back to `briefed` for a fresh round —
`recertify` refuses (spent), `block transition ... recertification-refused` refuses (one-door), and
`block transition ... approve` also refuses (block A's own one-door rule, block is already
`approved`). `land` is the only transition `BlockFlowTransitions` will accept from this state, and
nothing checks `reviewed_state` against the block's actual current content before permitting it. A
block that has been amended past what was certified can only be landed — the exact inversion of
what §8 exists to prevent, and the same species of defect as block B's stranding blocker (a state
with no correct exit), except here the wrong exit is available rather than none being available,
which is worse: it fails open rather than failing closed.

I don't think this is a worker slip — the worker implemented ruling 3 (`approved` gains exactly
*one* edge, singular) and ruling 5 (a successful recertification moves nothing but
`reviewed_state`) exactly as briefed, and both rulings are stated as binding in the block C brief.
This reads as a gap in the design those two rulings jointly produced: the "at most one
recertification per approval" bound has no corresponding "and here is how you get a new approval to
recertify against" edge once the one shot is spent successfully (the refused-recertification path
*does* get you a new round and a new approval automatically; the successful-recertification path
does not, and cannot, under the current table). **Fix-before-land, and I'd raise it as ❓
@architect rather than hand it back as a pure implementation defect** — the fix may be a design
call (does `land` need to validate `reviewed_state` against something? does a successful
recertification need its own way back to `briefed` for a *further* amendment, distinct from the
refused-claim path? is "one recertification, ever, full stop, land or refuse" actually the intended
reading and the refusal message's own "requires a new round" wording is the thing that's wrong?) —
not something the worker should improvise past the brief's explicit rulings without a fresh ruling.

**2. The two scoping mechanisms (claim set by `Round`, "already recertified" by approve-transition
timestamp) — checked for disagreement, found none in any reachable state, but the two are coupled
by construction rather than by a shared derivation, which is exactly the shape that has produced
this section's other two defects.**

- **Two approvals within one round** — unreachable. `RecordApprovalUnderExistingLock` only succeeds
  when `"approve"` is in `BlockFlowTransitions.AvailableFrom(currentState)`
  (`CardStore.cs:448–452`), which is true only from `in-review`. The only edges that return a card
  to `in-review` are `submit-for-review` (from `building`, no round change) — and there is no edge
  from `approved` back to `in-review` at all; the two edges from `approved` are `land` (terminal)
  and `recertification-refused` (`approved → briefed`, `round += 1`). So a second `approve` is
  always preceded by a round increment. Confirmed, not merely argued: `BlockRecertify_
  SecondAttemptAgainstTheSameApproval_Refuses` and `BlockRecertify_AfterARefusalAndAFreshApproval_
  PermitsANewRecertificationScopedToTheNewClaims` both exercise this and pass.
- **A successful recertification (round unchanged)** — both scopes agree by construction: `Round`
  doesn't move, `approvedAt` doesn't move (no new `"approve"` transition), so `currentClaimIds` is
  unchanged and the freshly-appended recertification comment is correctly seen as "since the current
  approval" on any subsequent attempt (correctly refusing it, per finding 1's own trace).
- **Round advanced by a refused recertification between approvals** — the case
  `BlockRecertify_AfterARefusalAndAFreshApproval_PermitsANewRecertificationScopedToTheNewClaims`
  exercises directly: both `Round` and the most-recent-`"approve"`-transition timestamp move
  together, at the same event (a fresh `approve`), so the stale round-1 recertification comment is
  correctly excluded from round-2's window and the stale round-1 claim id is correctly excluded from
  round-2's claim set. I traced this rather than only reading the test: the *only* place `Round`
  changes on the way back into `approved` is the refusal edges before the next `approve`, and the
  *only* place a new `"approve"` transition is appended is `RecordApprovalUnderExistingLock` itself
  — the two are not independently derivable from different data because everything that can move one
  necessarily also re-enters through the site that produces the other.

**Why I'm not calling this clean without a caveat.** The reason the two never disagree is that
`Round` and "most recent approve transition" happen to always move together given today's table —
not because either query is derived from the other, or from one shared "current approval" concept.
`CardCommentRouting.HasRecertification`'s own doc comment already names the general principle
("caller narrows the slice, this type never filters by round itself") but the two callers in
`RecordRecertificationUnderExistingLock` narrow that slice by two different keys (a round number, a
transition timestamp) that happen to be safe today only because nothing else in the table can move
one without moving the other. If a future block adds any edge that changes `Round` without going
through the `approve`-transition-then-refusal cycle (or vice versa), this pair silently drifts back
into the same species of bug this section has now produced twice. **Not a blocker** — I traced every
reachable state and found no live disagreement, and the round-boundary tests genuinely exercise the
coupling — but worth a note for whoever next touches `BlockFlowTransitions` or `RecordRecertification`.

**Standing checklist:**

- **Every claim receives an outcome; refusal names the ones left without one.** `MissingClaimOutcomes`
  (`CardStore.cs:588–592`) is named in the CLI refusal message (`CommandDispatcher.cs:1326–1329`),
  tested by `BlockRecertify_MissingClaimOutcome_Refuses_NamesTheOmittedClaim_
  AndLeavesTheCardByteIdentical`. Three-claim scenario matches the spec's own scenario exactly
  (`BlockRecertify_OneClaimRefused_...`: three claims, one refused, all three outcomes recorded in
  the response, `reviewed_state` untouched, `briefed`, `round` +1).
- **Refused recertification: byte-identical `reviewed_state`, no re-stamp, back to `briefed`, `round`
  +1, all outcomes recorded.** Confirmed by code (`CardStore.cs:539–551`) and by the test above.
- **Successful recertification: re-stamps `reviewed_state`, does not increment `round`.** Confirmed
  by code (`CardStore.cs:526–537`) and `BlockRecertify_EveryClaimAsserted_Succeeds_
  ReStampsReviewedStateWithoutIncrementingRound`.
- **8.13 — role-bound to reviewer/supervisor, reusing `IsApprovingRole`, no second predicate.**
  Confirmed (`CardStore.cs:544–547`, first check, ahead of `File.Exists`, same ordering as block

The reviewer was right to address it to `@architect` rather than to the worker: nothing in block C was

round" and defined **no transition delivering one**. After a successful recertification the block sat

The alternative considered and rejected was routing every failed recertify through
`recertification-refused`. It would have delivered the new round for free, but it required splitting
refusals into two species — those that move the card and those that do not — and every other verb in
this codebase holds the line that a refusal leaves the record untouched. That line is worth more than
the saved edge.

**[architect]** **Product Owner session on the process model — recorded, and carved as §8a.**

The question that started it: when the supervisor pushes back a second time, is that a repeat of the
previous remediation block or a new one? Answering it exposed that the supervisor loop is **almost
entirely unmodelled**. `supervisor` appears in the specs as a role that may approve and a verdict
recorded against a section; the section-level remediation *cycle* — what a pushback produces, what a
second one produces, when it stops — existed nowhere but in `CLAUDE.md` prose.

**Product Owner rulings:**

1. **A supervisor pushback is on the *section*, not on a block — so it creates a new card.** Its findings
   include drift *between* blocks, which belongs to no single block and has nothing to reopen. Each
   further pushback creates a further card.
2. **Reviewer-approved blocks are "semi-approved" — Schrödinger's kanban.** They sit in `approved` and do
   **not** officially land until the whole section is signed off by the supervisor.
3. **Third and fourth remediation rounds are routinely authorised** and the two-round cap does not
   reflect practice.

**What was actually built vs. what was decided.** Verified before recording: `CloseSection` touches only
the section card and never looks at a block, and `land` is an individually invocable per-block edge. So
today a supervisor could `request-changes` on a section whose blocks had **all already landed** — the
tool could only record that the process had been violated, which is precisely the incumbent failure this
project exists to replace. The model as decided makes the supervisor's verdict load-bearing.

**`approved` already is the semi-approved state**; no eighth state is needed. What changes is that `land`
stops being something the architect does to a block and becomes a consequence of section close.

**On the cap — the units were wrong, and our own practice was the evidence.** "Two rounds, then stop" was
overridden by the Product Owner twice *in this change* (§6 and §7), and is routinely overridden. A rule
that is routinely overridden is worse than no rule: it trains everyone to read the refusal as a
formality. But a third remediation round is not a *process violation* — it is a Product Owner decision.
So the tool refuses an **unauthorised** third round, names the authorisation that would satisfy it (9.1's
own refusal format), and permits an authorised one with its reason recorded. The override stops being a
chat message and becomes part of the record. Note `CLAUDE.md`'s cap has also been quietly incoherent
throughout — *"after one remediation block, do not carve a third"* — which is some evidence it was never
expressed in the right units.

**Recorded as:**

- `design.md` **D9** — approval is provisional; blocks land when their section closes.
- `specs/work-lifecycle/spec.md` — the existing "Remediation is the same card at a higher round" is
  **scoped to the reviewer loop** and renamed, because as written it forbade exactly what ruling 1
  decides. Three new requirements added: *Approval is provisional until the section closes*, *Section
  remediation is a new card*, *Remediation beyond the second round requires recorded authorisation*.
- `tasks.md` — new **§8a "Provisional approval and section-driven landing"**, 8a.1–8a.11.

**§9 renumbered.** Old 9.2 (*refuse landing where `reviewed_state` does not match*) and 9.3 (*refuse
landing on any non-zero or absent expected gate*) are landing refusals, and landing now happens inside
section close — so they moved into §8a as 8a.5/8a.6 rather than being built twice in two places. §9's
remaining tasks renumbered 9.1–9.10. **Nothing had been implemented against the old §9 numbers**, so no
commit or DEVLOG post references them.

**§8 is unaffected.** Block certification does not care when a block lands, so blocks A–C stand and block
D proceeds. §8a runs after §8 closes.

the findings" without saying it is a new card, and it still states the two-round cap as a prohibition.

**[architect]** **Product Owner refinement — section remediation routes by the finding, not by the
verdict.** This corrects what I recorded an hour ago, which was wrong in two ways.

The two scenarios at a supervisor review that includes a remediation:

- **the finding is still not resolved** → push **that card** back: it returns to `briefed` with `round`
  incremented, on the same card;
- **the finding is resolved but a new one is identified** → carve another card, because nothing owns the
  new finding.

**What I had recorded was wrong.** I wrote *"Each further `request-changes` verdict against the same
section SHALL create a further card"* — which makes a recurrence spawn a second card for a finding that
already has one, scattering one finding's history across N cards. And I wrote that a supervisor *"SHALL
NOT reopen any block the reviewer already approved"*, which forbids exactly the recurrence push, since a
remediation card **is** a reviewer-approved block. Both corrected.

**The refinement makes the model smaller, not bigger.** I had recorded the section loop as a *different*
rule from the reviewer loop. It isn't. The single rule underneath both is: **a card is the unit of work
for a finding; a finding that recurs stays with its card; a finding that is new needs one.** The reviewer
loop is that rule where the finding is always already owned; the section loop is that rule where it may
not be. `work-lifecycle`'s "remediation is the same card at a higher round" is general after all — I
scoped it to the reviewer loop this morning on the strength of my own wrong reading, and it now reads as
the general principle with the section loop as a case of it rather than an exception to it.

A supervisor still never reopens a **task-implementing** block: a first-time finding is new by
definition, and a recurrence targets the remediation card that was meant to close it. That is now a
refusal (8a.11), not a convention.

**New transition: `finding-recurred`** (`approved → briefed`, `round += 1`) — the only transition a
supervisor drives directly. Distinct from `amendment-requested` despite the identical From/To, by the
precedent now set four times over: the name is persisted in the card's history, and recording a
supervisor's recurrence push as an architect's amendment would misreport what happened. `approved` now
has four edges.

**The cap's units changed again, and this time for a reason the refinement exposed.** I had it counting
remediation *cards*. Under the refinement that bound is not total: a section can fail to converge by the
same finding recurring round after round after round, creating **no new cards at all**, and sail past a
card-counting cap untouched. It now counts the section's `request-changes` **verdicts** — which sees
accumulating findings, a recurring finding, and both at once. Derived from the section's retained
verdicts at request time, never stored (consistent with §10's "refuse any hand-entered count").

**Recorded as:** `work-lifecycle` — "Section remediation is a new card" replaced by "Section remediation
follows the finding, not the verdict"; the cap requirement recounted by verdicts with a scenario pinning
the recurring-finding case; `finding-recurred` added to the flow diagram and prose. `design.md` D9
updated. `tasks.md` §8a grows to 8a.1–8a.16.

`VALIDATE_EXIT:0`.

**[architect]** **`round` stays stored, and gains the invariant it never had.** Product Owner ruling.

The question that surfaced it: is there a counter of push-backs, or a log of state changes? Both, since
§5 — `BlockCardFields.Round` is the counter, and `CardFile.Transitions` is the append-only log, each
entry carrying the acting role, the transition's **name**, its from/to states and its timestamp.

Worth noting what the naming discipline bought here. Because every new edge got its own name rather than
reusing an existing one, the log does not merely say a block was pushed back five times — it says which
five things happened and who did each. Had `fix-before-land` been allowed to reuse `changes-requested`
(the cheap option at the time), that distinction would be **permanently** absent from the record, not
recoverable later. Same for `finding-recurred` against `amendment-requested`, which share From/To exactly.

**The hole.** `round` is now derivable — one plus the count of round-incrementing transitions — so it is
a stored figure duplicating reconstructible state, with nothing checking the two agree. That is the
failure this change has already legislated against twice: `work-lifecycle`'s own "Blocked is derived, not
stored", and §10's 10.9 "refuse any attempt to store a hand-entered count" with 10.8's "every figure
computed at request time". `round` predates four of the five transitions that now increment it; when §5
wrote it, `changes-requested` was the only one and it was nearly trivially correct. Every edge added
since is another place a write can bump the field without appending to the log, or the reverse.

**Ruling: keep it stored.** It is genuinely load-bearing on the wire — `GateResult.Round` pins gate
evidence to the round it was recorded in, which is what lets `GateStatusOf` tell "passed this round" from
"passed a round ago and nothing has re-run it since". Deriving it everywhere would buy consistency at the
cost of churn through evidence that has to stay a stored number anyway.

**So the assumption becomes a checked invariant** rather than disappearing. New requirement, *Stored
round agrees with the transition history*: the field equals one plus the round-incrementing transitions,
both advance in **one** write, and a card where they disagree is **refused, not repaired**.

The refuse-don't-repair part is the load-bearing half. Neither figure is privileged — a count ahead of
the history and a history ahead of the count are *different* failures with different causes, and
silently reconciling to either one destroys the evidence of whichever was actually right. This is the
same instinct as §7's duplicate-id resolution refusing rather than picking, and it is the whole thesis of
the tool: refuse where the incumbent could only record that something had gone wrong.

`tasks.md` §8a gains 8a.17 (the refusal) and 8a.18 (the one-write test). `VALIDATE_EXIT:0`.

**[architect]** **Block D brief — 8.11, 8.12.** The mechanical preconditions, as refusals and only as
refusals. **Last block of §8**; the supervisor review over `afaad73..HEAD` follows it.

**Tasks**

- 8.11 Implement the mechanical preconditions as refuse-only: gates re-run green, difference confined to
  nit sites
- 8.12 Test that green preconditions confer no claim until a reviewer asserts it

**Binding spec — `review-certification`, "Recertification is bounded"** (block C implemented the first
half of this same requirement; you implement the rest of it, so read it whole):

> Mechanical preconditions SHALL gate recertification and SHALL be able only to refuse it, never to
> satisfy it: every gate on the card SHALL have been re-run to a passing exit code, and the difference
> between certified and amended states SHALL be confined to the sites of the dispositioned nits. A
> difference extending beyond those sites SHALL send the block to full re-review, by the same
> `amendment-requested` route: the precondition refuses, and the architect reopens the block.

and, from the same requirement, the distinction block C already implements and you must not blur:

> A **refused recertification attempt** — one barred by the bound above, by a mechanical precondition,
> by the acting role, or by a malformed request — is not a verdict at all: it SHALL leave the card
> byte-identical, recording nothing and moving nothing.

Scenarios: *Out-of-scope difference forces full re-review* (refuses, leaves the card untouched, **names
`amendment-requested`**); *Green preconditions do not confer approval* (proceed permitted, **no claim
recorded as re-asserted until the reviewer asserts it**).

**The two facts this block needs and will not otherwise find**

- **The tool does not shell out.** `System.Diagnostics.Process` appears nowhere in `src/Callboard`, and
  this block does not introduce it. "Gates re-run green" reads the `GateResult`s already recorded on the
  card; it does **not** run `make gates`. "Difference confined to nit sites" compares **caller-supplied**
  changed paths against sites recorded on the card; it does **not** run `git diff`.
- **Nit sites are already on the wire.** Block B stored them on the nit-raising comment
  (`CardComment.Sites`, `CardCommentNitFieldKeys.Sites`) specifically so this block would not have to
  retrofit the format. Nothing reads them back today — you are the first reader. No wire change needed
  and none wanted.

**Architect readings and calls — binding; challenge in-thread if you think one is wrong**

1. **Changed paths arrive as `--changed <path>`, repeatable, and are required.** Same shape as
   `--assert`/`--refuse` in `ParseBlockRecertify`. Omitting it is refused at parse time (own refusal
   code, e.g. `changed-paths-required`) with a message saying the caller must state the paths the
   amendment touched. Do **not** treat "no `--changed`" as "an empty difference, vacuously confined" —
   that would turn the precondition off by omission, which is exactly the failure a refuse-only gate
   must not have.

2. **The gate precondition, precisely.** For every **distinct label appearing anywhere in
   `BlockCardFields.GateResults`** (any round — that is "every gate on the card"),
   `GateStatusOf(label).Passed` must be true. Refuse naming the labels that fail it, and keep the two
   failing reasons distinguishable in the message: *absent at this round* and *recorded non-zero* are
   different facts, and `GateStatus` was built to keep them apart — do not collapse them into "not
   green" in the text the reviewer reads.

3. **Be honest about what the gate precondition cannot check.** `GateResult` carries no timestamp, and a
   successful recertification does not move `round`, so a gate recorded *before* the amendment is
   indistinguishable from one re-run *after* it. This check therefore establishes "this round's gates
   are green", not "the gates were re-run since the amendment". **Do not add a timestamp to
   `GateResult`** to close that — it is a wire-format change to a §5 type, out of this block's scope, and
   it needs a Product Owner call. **Do not add a `--gates-rerun` flag or any affordance implying the tool
   verified freshness.** State the limit plainly in the doc comment, and surface it to the reviewer in
   `BlockRecertifyResult.Notice` alongside the re-derivation obligation block C already put there. This
   is the same call as block C item 7: refuse what we can, be honest about what we cannot, never record
   a promise as if it were evidence.

4. **The nit-site set is scoped to the current round.** The sites that bound this amendment are those of
   the nits **dispositioned in the round that produced the current approval** — not every nit the card
   has ever carried. An earlier round's nits name sites that are no longer under a live disposition, and
   admitting them silently widens the permitted difference. Derive the boundary from the record, the way
   block C derived "since the current approval": the current round starts at the timestamp of the **most
   recent transition whose `To` is `briefed`**, or `DateTimeOffset.MinValue` if the card has none. Take
   nit comments at or after that boundary that are dispositioned (`CardCommentRouting.
   IsNitDispositioned`), and union their `Sites`.

5. **Site matching, precisely.** Sites are free text a reviewer typed; they are not validated paths and
   you must not start validating them. Normalise both sides for comparison only: trim, replace `\` with
   `/`, and take a site's path portion as everything before its first `:` (so `src/Foo.cs:42` bounds
   `src/Foo.cs`). A changed path is **confined** if, for some site, it is ordinal-equal to that path or
   sits under it as a directory prefix (`site + "/"`). Any changed path matching no site refuses the
   attempt, naming **the offending paths** and the sites that were in bounds — the reviewer needs to see
   both to tell a real out-of-scope edit from a mistyped site.

6. **No dispositioned nits ⇒ the bound is empty ⇒ every changed path is out of scope ⇒ refuse.** Do not
   special-case it into a pass. A recertification exists because nits were dispositioned; a card with
   none has nothing bounded to amend, and full re-review is the correct route.

7. **The out-of-scope refusal must name `amendment-requested`.** The spec says so in the requirement text
   *and* in the scenario. Name the transition by its wire name in the refusal message, as the route to
   full re-review.

8. **Two new refusal-shaped cases on `CardRecertificationOutcome`** — one per precondition (e.g.
   `GatesNotGreen`, `DifferenceOutsideNitSites`), carrying the facts each message needs. Both are
   caller-correctable refusals, not `CardCorrupt` and not `ToolFailure`; both leave the card
   **byte-identical**. Every existing `Match` caller gains the two arms — that is the type doing its job.

9. **Ordering: the preconditions are evaluated last, immediately before the write.** After
   `UnknownClaimIds` and `MissingClaimOutcomes`. A caller who mistyped a claim id should be told they
   mistyped a claim id, not told about gates. Everything still refuses before anything is written.

10. **Refuse-only is a structural property, not a comment.** There must be no path on which a
    precondition *contributes* to an outcome: no claim marked asserted because the gates were green, no

**[architect]** **Block D is reviewer-approved but cannot commit green — and the blocker is a §6 test,
diagnosed.** `make gates` → `GATES_EXIT:2`, `TEST_EXIT:2`, 730/731, twice under my own hand and twice

`CardFindingRecordConcurrencyTests.WhenTheRaisedLockIsUnavailable_TheFindingLockIsReleasedBetweenRetries_NotHeldWhileWaiting`
(§6 block B's fifth remediation). It is green standalone, 3/3 here. It is **not** a rare flake: it fails
every full-suite run on this machine.

**Both the worker and the reviewer read it as scheduler contention degrading the test's timing
thresholds. That read is right about the cause and wrong about the mechanism**, and the mechanism is
what makes the fix obvious. The assertion that fails is not one of the two thresholds anyone predicted
(the `<300ms` probe or the `<4s` budget) — it is the test's own **precondition** at line 223:

> `Assert.False(recordTask.IsCompleted, "the call finished before the probe below could run — the planted lock was not actually blocking it.")`

Contention makes a call *slower*, so a load story that ends in "the probe took too long" does not explain
a call **finishing early**. The actual mechanism is in the test's own timeline:

```
await Task.Delay(400ms)            // intended: call is 400ms into a 3s retry budget
Assert.False(recordTask.IsCompleted)
```

The 400ms delay is only meaningful *relative to* the call's 3s budget, and both are wall-clock. Under a
contended full suite the delay overshoots — and the test's recorded duration says by how much: **3s 085ms
and 3s 126ms** on the two failing runs. A precondition that fired at ~400ms would end the test in well
under a second. It fired at ~3s, by which time the call had legitimately exhausted its whole 3s budget
and returned the honest `ToolFailure` the test goes on to assert. **The mechanism under test behaved
correctly on every failing run.** The test lost its race with itself.

**So this is a test defect, not a product defect.** Nothing in block D touches `CardLock` or
`RecordFinding` — the reviewer confirmed that independently — and the §6 release-between-retries property
this test exists to prove is not in question; the run that failed is a run in which it held. What is
wrong is that the proof is staged against wall-clock deadlines that only hold on an idle machine, which
is the same class of defect as a green test over a real one: here, a red test over working code.

**This is a Product Owner call and I am not making it unilaterally**, because the fix is §6 code while §8
is mid-close, and because "commit anyway, the failure is unrelated" is exactly the reasoning this repo's
`LABEL_EXIT` discipline exists to refuse. Block D itself is done: reviewer `Approve`, `BUILD_EXIT:0`,
`FORMAT_EXIT:0`, `VALIDATE_EXIT:0`, and 730/731 with the only failure diagnosed above. It is uncommitted
and unticked, waiting on that call.

**[architect]** **Remediation block — §6 test hardening (test-only, no new task numbers, ticks
nothing).** Product Owner's call on the diagnosis above: fix the red-over-working-code test *before*
block D commits, so block D lands on a genuinely green gate set rather than on my assurance that a red
gate was unrelated. Commits as its own `fix(...)`, ahead of block D.

**Scope: `tests/Callboard.Tests/CardFindingRecordConcurrencyTests.cs` and nothing else.** No production
code. The §6 release-between-retries property is **not** in question and must not be weakened — every
failing run was a run in which the mechanism behaved correctly. You are fixing the *proof*, not the
thing proved. Deleting the test, marking it `Skip`, or loosening a threshold until it stops failing are
all refusals of the task, not solutions to it.

**The defect, precisely.** `WhenTheRaisedLockIsUnavailable_TheFindingLockIsReleasedBetweenRetries_NotHeldWhileWaiting`
stages its proof as a wall-clock race against the call's own budget: it sleeps 400ms and then asserts the
call (budget 3s) has not finished. Under a contended full suite the sleep overshoots to ~3s, the call has
legitimately exhausted its budget, and the precondition fails. Both figures are wall-clock and only
meaningful relative to each other, which is why it is green standalone and red every full-suite run.

**The fix — make the ordering structural instead of temporal.** Two calls, both binding:

1. **Give the blocked call a budget long enough that no overshoot can consume it** — seconds of sleep
   slop must not be able to reach it (30s is the right order; the call never actually spends it, because
   the planted lock is released or the test ends first). Then "the call has not finished" stops being a
   race: while the planted lock is held by this live process, the call *cannot* complete, so the
   precondition is true by construction rather than by arriving in time.

2. **Make the load-bearing probe assert a ratio the lock itself measures, not a stopwatch you read.**
   Blocking-acquire the finding's own lock from outside the call with a timeout far below the call's
   budget, and assert it **succeeds**. That is already the real proof: if the finding's lock were held
   continuously for the whole retry loop (the defect), the acquire could not succeed until the call's
   budget ran out, so a timeout well under that budget refuses it. The `Stopwatch` and the `<300ms`
   comparison then carry no weight and should go — a threshold nobody's correctness depends on is a
   flake generator, and this one has now cost two review rounds.

**Split off the budget-exhaustion assertion rather than dropping it.** The current test also proves the
blocked call ends in an honest `ToolFailure` at its own declared timeout — worth keeping, and it does not
survive call 1 (a 30s budget makes waiting for exhaustion absurd). Give it its own `[Fact]`: plant the
lock, make one `RecordFinding` call with a short budget, await it, assert `ToolFailure` and that nothing
was written through the planted lock. **No interleaving, so no race** — that test has two events, not
three, and cannot lose an ordering it never depends on.

Keep both tests' doc comments carrying the reviewer's original "80 trials produced zero natural hits"
reasoning for why this is proved deterministically rather than by racing a window; that reasoning is
still exactly right, and this block is it being applied one level further out.

**run it more than once**, and say in your report how many full-suite runs you saw green, because a
single green run is precisely the evidence this test has been producing falsely all along. Block D's

**[reviewer]** §6 test-hardening remediation — **Request changes.**

**Scope confirmed.** `git diff d72d187` touches only `tests/Callboard.Tests/CardFindingRecordConcurrencyTests.cs`
plus this DEVLOG; the four production files carry the exact same insertion/deletion counts as my last
approved pass on block D (69/121/69/39 lines), and `CardCommentImmutabilityTests.cs`/
